• Le Gallic:4a relates a characteristic anecdote of Prince Bismarck. When a delegate to the Diet at Frankfort he lived in the house of one of the lead- ing inhabitants. His host refused to supply his guest with a bell in his bedroom—an omission which Bismarck supplied by discharging a pistol through the ceiling when he wished to ring for his . valet. "That is the way," said he to his frightened host, "that I shall continue to call my servant so long as I.have no bell." A bell was provided next day. . . . . .

The topic of the hour outside Parliament is the defeat of Slavin by Jackson, the coloured man, in the great prizefight for 42,000 f • Londoners pin their faith on Slavin, and are deeply grieved that he was knocked about so effectually and scieqifi- cally by Jackson. It was certainly the sorriest exhibition of pugilism London has witnessed. The admission tickets were ..C25 each. All spectators wore evening dress, and Lord Lonsdale ,presided over the exercises. j I •

That Lord Roberts had contributed a paper for the information of Lord Wantage'a Committee, set- ting forth his views on the state of the Army is a fact long familiar in military circles. Shortly after the session opened a question on the subject was put to Mr. Stanhope but no direct information was elicited. Lord Randolph Churchill is understood to have in his possession a full summary of the docu- ment which he was anxious of having an °oppor- tunity a alluding to in debate on:the Report,of the Committee.

. --,-- Mrs. Langtry drives every morning in the park , (says the "Lady's Pictorial") drawn by a big dark chestnut, which is quite a picture or what a single harness carriage-horse ought to be. She has a foot- man and coachman, in the neatest ot livery,and her usual companion is a black poodle, . shaved in the orthodox way, and having his forelock tied with pale blue ribbon. This goes well with his mistress's ,dark blue foulard gown printed with yellow, and her chip hat, black underneath, and straw co.our at the top, is trimmed with pink roses.,

"G. A. S." writes as to insomnia: "Everybody has his nostrum for sleeplessness. Dr. Franklin's was to get into another bed. Sir Henry Thompson, I have been told, if he is unable to sleep, gets up and paints. Dr. Benjamin Richardson prescribes a boiled Portugal onion for supper. But may Ibe permitted to put in a word in favour of a very old French antidote for insomnia—iv verre deau,to wit? This is something more than eau sucrec, the bever- age being-flavoured with a few drops of orange- flower water. The effect, to me, has always been inexpressibly soothing and 'reposeful. Try it."

, . The following hitherto unpublished anecdote tends to show that the Emperor William can at least "tell a hawk from a hernshaw." On the occasion of the Visit of the British fleet to Kiel the young Kaiser went on board the, flagship, and was particularly struck by the flne.-show of men. He remarked this to the captain, "Are they all your own, as I know you sometimes beat them, up from other ships on • these occasions?' The captain replied, so we are told, that in the present instance at least they were all on the books of the ship; but it was plain from the Emperor's question that he was up to the tricks of the trade.

We have heard a great deal lately of drunkards acquiring a permanent distaste for alcohol in Atnerica by what is culled the Keeley system, Dr. Keeley having discovered that subcutaneous injec- tions of gold in some form produce this result. The system has been adopted in the homes in which tl.e old soldiers of the American Civil War reside, and has been taken up by several States as a part of their charity organisations. lam glad, therefore, to hear that Dr. Keeley is over here, and proposes to open a cure institution at Weybridge. We shall thus hare an opportunity ot testing the method. If it really produces the alleged results, the discovery will be of the greatest possible benefit to the cause of temperance.

The barriers which have been impudently placed across Shakespeare's Avon by the tenant of Cherie- cote-park have just been again broken down. They were forced in April, and on that occasion the names of the "offenders" were taken by tAie land- lord's agent. Neither writs nor summonses,however, were issued. If the law were not in so defective a condition the courts wouldhave been occupied with the case long ago, but .the defendant would be— not some man who asserted his right to pass up the river in a boat, but—the landlord who dares to ob- struct nubile rights on a navigable river. it is mon- strous that this squire should be allowed to openly ' and persistently attempt to appropriate public pro- perty without running the risk. of a prosecution. Why does not the local authority interfere?

The usually sober and liberal "Siècle" roundly charges the London Press with supressing the truth shout the events of January laat in Uganda; and,accepting for once the word of a German news- paper correspondent, seeks, to hold Captain Lugard and the English missionaries, "who for years past have preached hatred of the Papists, "directly responsible for the masaacre of .50,000 native Catholics. "Note how the English hasten the march of civilisation : Note how they undertake the defence of the interests of Christianity !" These are not pleasant words; and though they do not yet bring, as their authors wish, the " blush of shame' to our cheeks, yet it is highly advisable that they should receive at once an atitharitative and categorical reply.

Lady Violet Ashley. who is to marry the Earl of Mar and Kellie, is the pretty granddaughter of the. celebrated philanthropist whose good work in behalf of the oppressed and injured women and children, and the poor generally, will he remem- bered when many other more sounding reputations are forgotten, and whose epitaph is stamped on the metropolis alone the length of Shaftesbury-avenue. Lord Mar and Keine is the heir of the more famous Lord Mar and Kale, whose dispute with the present Earl of Mat (then Mr. Goodeve Erskine) as to the right succession to the ancient Earldom of Mar, is one of the causes colebres of the• century, and fur- nished some dramatic scenes it the meetings for the election of Scotch representative peers. The present Lord Afar and Keine is a lieutenant in the Scots Guards, a Leen sportsman. and an ardent:deer- stalker.

div.head: DERBY.
div.p: THE DERBY.

The race for the Derby,on Wednesday, resulted in the easy victory of Lord Bradford's Sir Hugo,. a horse of which so little was thought that it was a:lowed to start at the odds of 40 to L The second place was obtained by Baron Hirsch's filly La Fleehe, which has held the position of favourite since the Duke of Westminster's colt Orme was withdrawn from the race as the result of events which have greatly agitated the turf world. The general opinion of the critics was that the three-year- olds this season are a very moderate lot, and one of the :major prophets declared so late as Monday last that Sir Hugo was not of the stuff of which Derby winners are made. That unreliable seer, however, has had reason to change his opinion. The "clock test "as applied to the winner of Wednesday's race shows that Sir Hugo , covered the Derby course in less time than Gladiateur or , °monde or Bend Or. L.O RD, WOLSELEY'S CIiMMUS PUDDING.

tOrd Wolseley amusingly tells in the "Strand Magazine" how he and a brother officer made their Christmas pudding in the Crimea. "We had no bread nor flour, only , biscuit, which we powdered up in a hollowed-out shell, with a shot for a pestle. No plums either.-- But we chopped up some figs,- And managed to get a couple of pounds of very bad Suet from Balaclava. We had some doubts in our minds as to whetlienit ought to be roasted or boiled, but finally decided on the latter, and wrapped our mixture up in a- towel. Now, in the ordinary course Of events it was not our turn for the ..renches, but the pudding had scarcely been boiling half an hour when an officer came and ordered us out. W hat was to be done? Eat the Christmas ooncoction now 07'4 to-morrow? Decision—now. And, unmindful a the fact that Christmas puddings take a great deal longer to boil, I contest; to eating liberally. Away; I went to the trenches. -About twelve o'clock .e thought I was going to expire. •It • Was the only night I ever had to leave the trenches. A regi- mental doctor got hold of me, and I was on my way home when the walk did me st; much good-that I. went back again: 'Since then I hlive never made a; Pudding, Christmas or otherwise." ,

THE. CAPTAIN OF THE WARRINGTON . . --CRICKET CLUB. The following is an extract from'a special article in the "Manchester Examiner and Times" of Satur- day last, on the Captain of the Warrington Cricket Club:- 21r!gydnetliorland Crosfield yeti )3clrit. at War- rington on November 12tb, 1861, and is by-profes- sion a solicitor. Ile was educated at Wimbledon, nnd during his stay there, kiis cricket proclivities gave evident promise qf dnisething ate the aver- age, and he was singularly:, tuacessftil;heading the batting tables one season. Leaving school he quickly turned his early training to good account, and his all-round abilities Were speedily recognized by the County Committee who invited him to rep- resent his County v. Oxford University 'in June. 1883, and he contributed two splendid innings'of 43 and 49. His runs on that occasion were obtained ' stylishly and with no small_ amount of confidence, and agreat future was predicted for him. He sub- sequently made 32 in the return y. Oxford, 25 v. Derbyshire, and 19 v. Notts, andide altogether 176 runs in 10 innings, an average'over 17 runs, which was moss encouraging to a first season's player. The summer of 1884 saw.but very little of him in the cricket field, his time being altogether taken up in working for an examination in connec- tion with his profession. in season 1885 lie was persuaded to assist Cheshire undeethe feiidential qualification, and althou,,li his severance from first- class cricket was regrettable at the time when, his form and experience would have benefitted largely by his continuance, he proved a valuable addition to the cheese county,and for four seasons, up to the end of 1888, he rendeOed excellent service as besides his batting his fielding was superb, and he bore. the onerous duties of captaincy with considerable credit. His best scores were 52,n0t but, v. York- shire (a meritorious display, as going in first lie carried his bat right through the innings) and 52 v. Lancashire. During his connection with Cheshire he became identified with the Cheshire Gentlemen, and scored hugely on many occasions. He made 122 v. the Gentlemen of Notts, 91 and 56 v. Yorkshire Gents, and in 1887 he had a grand batting average of over 60 for them. In 1888 he again renewed his relations with Lancashire cricket. He is a most enthusiastic and uncommonly keen club cricketer. He divides his time when free from county cricket with the Warrington, Sefton, and Manchester clubs. Ile is captain of the former team, and has much to do with its successful posi- tion, scoring a lot of runs and being very popular. ' For Warrington v. Sefton he made-100 last season, while the Manchester and Sefton clubs bendit ' largely .by his services. Mr. Sydney Moreland Crosfield has since his withdrawal from the Cheshire team given his services to Lancashire in the most ungrudging manner possible. He has proved a singularly able lieutenant to the present great captain, and he possesses many of the traits of character which have so distinguished Mr. Hornby and made him famous as one of the greatest cricket leaders of the age. Mr. Crosfield is a keen and determined-player, and in the field or at the wicket he works with an honesty of purpose that acts likes magnet to those who are at times andel Ms command. Ile has a very easy and attractive style, and when he dces get going he makes runs quickly. He is particularly powerful on the off side, and low -driving and cutting are special .feataree. He watches the ball very closely, &Ai as a consequende his defence is at times difficult to get through. In local cricket he is occs.sionally called upon tolxiwl, and does not by any means do it badly, bowling right hand medium pace, and is very smart in fielding his own bowling.

div.p: STORIES FROII THE " -

Alessrs. F. Warne and Company publish in their i` Chandos Classics" (price 25.), selection's from' thef; " Talm ad,' translated from the original by F. Polano, professor of the Hebrew language. The "Talmud" , May be described as a Jewish encyclopedia of law,' civil and penal, human and divine. It not only con- tains commentaries and teachings, but poetry and legends. We give two selections from the latter, which are as follows : THE LAWFUL HEIR.

A wise Israelite, dwelling some distance from Jerusalem, sent his son to the Holy City to complete his education. During his son's absence the father was taken ill, and feeling that death was upon him he made a will, leaving all his property to one of his slaves, on condition that he should allow the son to select any one article wkich pleased him for an inheritance. As soon as his master died, the slave, elated with his good fortune, hastened to Jerusalem, informed his late master's son of what had taken place, and showed him the will. The young man was surprised and grieved at the intelligeece, and after the allotted time of mourning had expired, he began to seriously consider his situ- ation. He went to his teacher, explained' the cir- cumstances to him, read him his father's will, and expressed himself bitterly on atcount of the disap- pointment of his reasonable hopes and expectations. He could think of nothing that he bad done to offend his father, and was loud in his complaints of injustice. "Stop," said his teacher. " thy father was a man of wisdom and a loving relative. This will is a living mouutnent to his good sense and far-sighted- ness. May his son prove as wise in his day." "' What !" exclaimed the young men. "I 601 no wisdom in his bestowal of his property upon a slave no affection in this slight upon his only ion." "Listen," returned the teacher'. "By this action thy father bath but secured thy inheritance to thee, if thou art ,wise enough to avail thyself of this understanding. Thus thought he when he felt the hand of death approaching: My son is away; when I am dead he will not be here to take charge of my affairs; my slaves will plunder my estate, and to gain time will even conceal my death from my son, and deprive me of the sweet savour of mourning.' To prevent these things he bequeathed his property to his slave, well knowing that the slave, believing in his apparent right, would, give ' the speedy information and take care of the effects, even as he has cone." "Well, welltand how does this benefit me?" im- patiently interrupted the pupil. "Ah l" replied the teacher, "wisdom I see rests not with the young., Dost thou not know that what a slave possesses belongs but to his master? Has not thy father left thee the right to select ,one article of all his property for thy own? Choose the slave as thy portion, by possessing him thou wilt recover all that was thy father's. Such was his wise and-loving Intention." The young man did as he was advised, and gave the slave his freedom afterwards. But ever after he was wont to exclaim: "Wisdom resides with the aged, and understand- ing in length of days."

NOTHING IN THE WORLD WITHOUT ITS USE. David, King of Israel, was once lying upon his couch and many thoughts were passing through his mind. , "Of what use in this world is the spider ? " thought he; "it but increases the dust and dirt of the world, making places unsightly and causing great annoyance." Then be thought of an insane man. "How unfortunate is such a beiag. I know that all things are • ordained by God with reason and purpose, yet this is beyond tny comprehension ; who should men be born idots, or grow insane ? " Then the mosquitoes annoyed him, and the king thought: "What can the mosquito be good for? why was it created in the world? It hut disturbs our com- fort, and the world profits not by its exhtence." let King i•avid lived to discover that these very insects' and the very condition of life, the being of which he deplored, were ordained wren to his uwn benefit. When he fled from before Saul, David was cap- tured in the land of tbe Philistines by the brothers of Goliath,who carried him before the king of Oath, and it was only by pretending idiocy that be escaped death, the king deeming it impossible that such a man could be the kingly David; as it is written, and he disguised his reason before their eyes, allot played the madman in their bands, and scribbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle run down upon his beard" (Sam. 21: Upon another occasion David hid himself in the cave of Adullam, and after he had entered the cave it chanced that a spider spun a web over the open- ing thereto. His pursuers passed that way, but thinking that no one eould have entered the cave protected by the spider's web with Jut destroying it they continued on their way. • , The mo•Rquito also was of service to David when he entered the camp of Saul to secure the lattees weapon. While stooping near Abner, the sleeping ' man moved and placed his leg upon David's body. If he moved, he would awake Abner and meet ' with death,if he remained in that position morning would dawn and bring him death ; he knew not what to do, when a mosquito alighted, upon, . Abner's leg; he moved it quickly, and David escaped. ' Therefore sang David: " All my bones shall say, 0 Lord who is like un- to Thee."

div.head: MR. MICHAEL DAVITT ON IRELAND.
div.p: MR. MICHAEL DAVITT ON IRELAND.

Mr. R. Leake, M.P., and Mr. Michael Davitt addressed a Liberal meeting at Radcliffe on Saturday night. Mr. Davitt answered in detail a number of arguments ad- vanced by opponents of Home Rule. Ile quoted figures from a blue-book of Mr. Balfour's to show that Ireland had not increased in material .prosperity udder Tory rule. In 1860, with a population of six millions, there were 170,549 persons in Irish workhouses. In 1890, with a population of 4,6000,000, there were 334,168 persons in the workhouses. Mr. Davitt also quoted figures to show that Ireland contributed its full share to the Imperial revenue.

div.p: ,AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF ENGINEMEN, r

FORMATION OF 'A BRANCH IT WARRVSGTON.. On Saturday night, a meeting was held at the Rope and Anchor Inn,Buttermarket-street, Warring- ton, for the purpose of forming a branch of the Amalgamated Society of enginetnen, cranemen, boilermen, and firemen, the headquartere of which is at Middlesboro' and which has been in existence about A years. There was not It laree attendance. Mi. G. Sambrook. presided. Mr. G. If Copley, No. 3 district secretary, of Rotherham, addressed) the meeting at considerable length on the advantages of joining the society, the objects of which, be said, were concilation, and not autagouism to the employers, and which numbered 50 branches and over 5,000 members. A branch' had been opened at Runcorn that morning with 31 members, and about 20 or 80 Of the team men there were going to join in a body. ,He pointed out certain abuses which existed in the trades whieli the society represented, and which it was its object to remedy. He complained of the system of employing hollermen and firemen at 18e. a week who did not understand their work instead of pay- ing 245. a week, and hiving competent men, and men- tioned the ease of a firm whip had by doing the latter, and having two men instead of one, saved 80 tons of coal a week, and through adopting Such principles had declared a dividend of A percent., thstigh not having previously had one for two years. At Hull, he said,the men employed in the trade bad been only paid single time for Sunday work, end the society had obtained for them double time for that day, and poncessions as. to overtirme. He- believed that the time would come when employers universally, would be convinced that 8 hours' work a day would be the best thing for themselves and their men. There was not an employer who had adopted the system that did not admit it was the best paying one. The mineral royalties were a drawback to both employers and employed. It was a 'question of who had a right to the minerals and the earth which contained them except those who laboured to extract them, but these royalty owners got all the money and did nothing for it. Lord St. Oswald had 12s. for every ton of ore derived from his land, and the worker only got 2s. Std. Was that a fair division of profit-? The sassrk- ing-men would never get a remedy for these things unless they. bound themselves together. Had they ever been 'fairly represented in Parliament? ("No:".) Why did they not demand from Parliament what they wanted. He dirt not believe in this bsgging and Praying to 'mem- bers of Parliament to do this and the other; let the working-men put their foot down and, say they would have to do it or they should not go 'to the Hone of Commons. (Applause.) It was useless to return men whtemerely went there to represent themselves- Did those present think that a maeufacturer would promote a Bill providing that boilermen should pass an •examina- tion before being allowed to take charge of boilers ? If workmen did not stir up and make an alteration„depend upon it the employers would stir them up and shake the life out of them. The speaker referred to the immense amount of surplus capital, and to Alm exist- ence.of millionaires as a curse to society, existing he said while there were 60,000 men out of employment in London streets. ,Tbere were 2,000 men out of work In. Bradford at present. It was time that the 'working- men bestirred themselves and demanded a fair rate for the labour they did. He maintained that unless' they banded themselves together to put an end to the present condition of things, there would in less than ten years be a revolution in this country. Fie could tellef a firm that decided that no man should be set on at their works who was over 35 years of age. Where were their grey-headed brothers to go to if thiewas to he allowed? What peevisiOn was there for tbeiened brethren except the miserable werkhouselp‘ As for visor law administra- tion, there was not one guardian in a thousand fit to hold his seat. The distribution of charitiee left for the poor also demanded investigation. Let the working classes demand parish councils and absolute control for them of all charities and royalty rents. The Conserva- tives, said Hie speaker, would never do anything for the masses; the Liberals had done the most, but they would find that when they came to the worst they would have to do it themselves. Mr. Copley concluded by strongly urging those present to join the society.— Several questions were answered by him, and Subse- quently a number enrolled themselves as membersef the new branch, and a committee and officers were elected pro fem.

THE CURSE-OF THE-CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN,
Author of "Some Fisher Folk?' "Judith?' "Where the North Wind Blows," cke., dec.

. ?CHAPTER 41.4V1. 7 .IitTURN OF JACK , Brown :' the lieutenant of: the Ixiastguaid; although a stern, was by no means an 'unjust man; and upon mature reflection he was inclined to place +credence in the death-bed revelation of Bill Wid- drington; and to exonerate Dick Diglish from any participation in the murder of Innes. Tantalising It undoubtedly was to have had one of the crew un- der his thumb as it were, and yet to have failed in eliciting the names of the rest; but innocent paglish was apparently, and there Was nothing to 'be gained by punishing the innocent fOr the ,
'guilty. Therefore the Lieutenant confined hiniself tO'the

performance of his duty, and sent a fall, but =- ' prejudiced account of matters to heb.dquarterif., The result of this proceeding was the withdrawal , of all proclamations against Dick, and the offer in- 'stead of a heavy sum for any reliable information about the true culprit or culprits. Dick was therefore free to. return whenever and . .
wherever he chose ; a permiesion of which he was nbt Slow to avail himself, he being by'Ehis time

very sick-of kicking his heels in the fishing ham- let upon the Scotch coast, whither he had fled after the discovery of the coastguard's fate. t._ Although a slight intimacy existed between the Burnmouth and the,Breamish fisher-folk, owing to the former adventuring south even as far as the mouth of the Tyne and tket port of Shields during the herring season in their keel or decked boats,' there was still: no great good will existing between them. : A noble contempt of " forriners" dwelt in ,the bosom of the Northumbrians, and foreigners. in- cluded all people born outside of O. radius of say twenty miles from their native village ; while the Scots for their part are known all the world over to possess the quality of clannishness in a higher degree than any Other nation. Therefore either set of fishermen and fisherwomen hugged them- selves with a consciousness of their own immense superiority, and the manners and customs of each were' held up to ridicule by the opposition party. If a Breamish lass were so far wiled from the path of duty ,as to be seen walking aleng the links with one of the young Scotchmen ; her mother or nearest feminine neighbour was q-uickte resent such a lowering 'of dignity, and to recall her speedily to a sense of the . proprieties by making it under- stood that to wed an alien :and a stranger would arouse great indignation and contempt in the place, awl wegll also cause a sundering of all, the ties qf lave and kTüliip, tiw)j,ich are always so exceedingly strong in these paaple. Mixed Marriages were therefore almost unknown, and the result of this exclusiveness is most probably the continuance of the original type—the fair hair, rudely scomplexions, and stalwart limbs of the arvdtiura,pr sea robbers, Iyho first invaded and settled upon these northern Shoies. Dick Daglish was a Breamish man born and bred, although his quick, dark eyes and vivacious manner suggested that in his case at some period or other of his family history, alien blood must have mingled with the original strain, and all his sym- pathies and prejudices were enlisted against the Barnmouth people, among sl- whom it was necessary for him to abide for a seSiop. He felt like a fish out of water. " Their very manner of living irked him • He tired of kail-brose and oatmeal porridge, and objected to being. shut up in a bed within a wall without a breath of air, and to eating singed sheep's head with the skin on, a dish that went sore against his stomach. The Scotch lassies cast longing eyes, at his gocil 'humoured and comely visage, but all in vain. He was blind to their charms. More than all things was he pining to see his bonny sweetheart, Bell, again. ' People did not rely in those days upon letters for their lovemaking, and sad to say, Dick could not write, although he could just manage to spell out printed words, always providing that they were words familiar to him. So he kept silence perforce, since he never , had a chance to send a verbal message, and, he would not condescend to ask help' to write to - I Bell.

--- Had he known, of course, what was going on in his salience, .and what torturing suspense his silence caused to Bell, this -state oethings would have been immediately altered. But that suspicion should ever fall upon him from such a quarter never once occurred to his mind. All the world might doubt him, but the lass he _loved would certainly hold him guiltless. Bell was loyal to the core of her big, generous heart, there was no doubt of that. But men take these long absences and silences differently from wonien, with greater calmness— more profound philosophy. To be sure their objective active lives do not give them the same opportunities for sad reflection, and for morbid anatomy, of motives. With so much of the work of women is done while sitting, or with slight action, they can pursue their mental work of dissecting, conjecturing, hunting motives, diagnosing eases from symptoms in a manner undreamt of by the leas complex-minded sex who are for the most part either too simple or too indifferent to penetrate below the seeming of things, and therefore save themselves endless trouble and pain. Constructive imaginations are not always a blessing; unless to a modern novelist, who must perforce ring the changes upon horrors in a manner unknown in more virile healthily minded times. • 'J3ell Widdrington was healthily minded enough; but she was a woman, and the woman's faculty for • self-torture had not been neglected in her com- position. When the message came at last to Dick that he was cleared of the imputation which had rested upon him, he assuredly did not require long to pre- pare for his return to Breamish. His heart was very full of hope and joy and love and sorrow too, as he took the familiar road along ' the links—the road leading to his sweetheart's home. Down in the village 'he had heard for the first time of the death of poor Bill Widdrington, the dearly loved twin brother of his dear lass, and he was sad because of the sadness he knew would he hers, besides his own ; for Bill's pleasant, sunny temper had won friendship from everyone, and from Dick especially, who saw Bell's fine lineaments reflected in the masculine visage of her brother, and who naturally loved them .here also.

'"Poor Bill! It's difficult to fancy him lyin' quiet and silent under the mools ! ' muttered Daglish under his breath, when old Carr tali him the news; with a passing wonder at the strange caprice of death in leaving those who were sick, or weak or sorrowful, and laying a detaining hand instead upon Bill's yellow curls, and quenching the light in his merry, roguish eyes. Then, aloud he went on, " Aw can hardly credit it o' BilL Him an' me had a long crack the day afore aw left, an' he seemed as lively as a gull in a thunderstorm! Not but what he was a bit changed i' them days, didn't lark aboot se much, and when he laughed laughed louder, maybe. Like me, aw darrsay gettin' a bit tired o' the life' when he'd a wife at home, an' would rather ha' been sittin' by the fire- side wi' her, than tossin' on the stormy sea or walkin' the deck o' the Bonny Bess. An' there's another blow! To think o' her gannin' be smash like yon on • Death's Ribs,' an me far away! There's neebody understood how to manage her so well as me, though it sounds like blowin' me Own trumpet te say so. Not that awm blamin' Bill, nor thinkin' that he'd blundered in anyway, for he was a right good sailor," Thor wee sneebeihr to blame, so thou needn't upcast either Bill or anybody else, ma man r broke in old Carr, in a deep growl; "the sloop's gaen te the bottom, as aw knew- to ma cost, for maist every penny aw bed i' the world wes sunk in her, but that would be small odds if only wor Bill had been left. Thor wee a black mark agy en the lot on us, an' his mates an' him, an' the Bonny Bess paid the reekonin'." The fisherman was leaning against a rail and gazing moodily over the harbour, as he talked to The latter was immediately struck with the strange tone, and looked at the old fisherman more attentively. Upon the seamed and weather beaten countenance of the ancient salt emotions had long since ceased to leave any trace. Like the figure head of the Medusa in Bell's kitchen, which, when the gilding had been once washed off it, had been incapable of showing any further ravages from the hand of time, old Carr's figurehead wore well, be- cause there was no longer any beanty in it to suffer-i deterioration. Joy or sorrow alike passed by, and left it unmoved and unaltered. Nevertheless, there was something not quite normal about the aspect of the old man something which arrested the attention, and roua‘d the wen- zaalg. A whafkLiaasatalanaaa iat& ania
t

ifwitcliffit th 4 muscres around th-e iiióiithth very pitiggasjavg fEibt that his pipe dangled uselessly, in his han-d=fillid, but unlighted. What ailed the old man? Here he was talking as though the wreck of the sloop would have been a slight matter if only his son-in-law's life had not -rne- with her, and yet a-keener hand at a bargain or a closer fisted man, taken altogether, Dick had never known. And what was thilhiitt he let fan, this hint at some reaSon why the loss of his sloop and of the lives aboard of her appeared just in his eyes? In an ordinary way, the last thing one Would have expected would have been to hear old Carr acknowledge any right in providence to deal with his goods and chattels as it chose; and many and deep were the curses he was wont to give vent to on the occasion of any misfortune or blunder which concerned the Bonny Bess; M Dick knew to his cost in his capacity of skipper.

And now to see the old fellow taking the very worst that could befall him and his so tamely roused Dick's extreme surprise and bewilder ment. " Awm the last man to upcast a man's misfor- tunes, more especially when the poor chap's paid for them wi' his life, but its hard on me too not to be in at the end, me that sailed her through all 'kinds of weather, and wes fond of every plank and timber that shewas made on !"_

"Ay, ay ! It's doobtless hard, but there's worse than that to bide, for some on us," responded old Carr, in an even monotonous bass. "Ye haven't got owt on yer conscience te blame yersel' for— leastways nowt wo.ur nor free tradin', an' that's nee sin surely !" "Sin or no, aw'in gann te give it up !" said Dick with 'd cision. He. expected to find his resolution meet with great opposition, for he had been the prime mover and the daring adventurer of the band, and old Carr had shown great appreciation of his services in the past, and had been the chief agent in tempting him to fresh ventures, and holding him fast to the life. , His surprise was therefore greater still when the announcement of this determination elicited noth- ing but a sullen acquiescence. Maybe ye're reet ? Anyway awm not gaen te argify the point wi' ye. For myser, aw'in owre and te alter ma ways; an' if some of oor cheps ven- tures another run, aw'll gan in wi' them still! But awm none for meddlin' wi' other folks, or forcin' , them agyen their wills. Aw've had about enough o' fightin' an' o' bad blood, an' o.w would fain be friends wi' all men—stivin'only th' Excise men, poor chops, And them aw'll rather run away from than face I" "I did not expect ye to take yer losses so easily, Mr. Carr," exclaimed Daglish, giving his astonish- ment a voice. , The fialaman szitched his head, and looked over the sea in silence.' Then he turned his pale restlesa eyes upon Dick's face, and they were full of a profound contempt for the want of discrimination displayed by the younger Man. "When ye reach ma time of life—if ever ye do, ma canny man—ye'll ha' learnt that it isn't,always the yens that cries loudest that's the midst hort I Wad ye ha' me blubber ower the loss o' the sloop, like a bairn ower its broken toy ?" Dick could make nothing out of the unaccustomed attitude of the old fisherman ; but after leaving him still standing there looking out to sea, and proceed- ing himself along the luiks, he soon ceased to marvel, because his mind was too full of thoughts of Bell to allow of any other occupation. Oh; but it Would be sweet to kiss the tears from off her beautiful face and to find her turn to him for consolation in her sorrow, and her affliction 1 He felt rather guilty, because the thrill of delight this gave him panetrated through all the natural grief and horror he +felt at poor Bill's untimely fillt transfused eiwn into his own regret a subtle sweetness. But he was not fated to reach the home of Beltin this dreamy, pleasant, bitter-sweet state of mind. When he arrived within sight a the cottage, he was aware of a biq dour-looking man who stood ip the pathway, barring his progress. With an ex- clamation of pleasure he held out his hand; whli the other, after some deliberation, accepted in a gingerly fashion, but allowed to drop, without the hearty grip and salutation common amongst the village folk. "Why, Cuddy man, what ails ye that ye glower at a friend, an' let his fist drop as though it were a rotten harrin' ? Hoos' ma canny Bell an' the granny. Are they sair put oot about poor Bill's death? But •aw needn't plc that, since aw know he was the flower o' the flock to the aad wife, an'' that ma Bell wasn't far ahind i' the love for him An' thou maun miss him badly too?" TAO gloomy expression deepened on the face of Bill's brother. He put his hand on Dick's shoulder, and, faced him right about. "Ye do wellte mind me o' Bill, an' the fate aw might ha' saved him from, had aw minded ma Bible an' ma conscie ice, lad, an' let the filthy lucre gan to the devil! But it's been a lesson te me, an' a lesson not learned in vain, aw hope. Awm the heed o' the family, an' therefore the haill o' the responsibility rests wi' me! Then 'sartainly aw mun take thowt for the rest. Dick Daglish, ye mun.\ turn yer steps back to Breamish, an' let ma sister be! Awm not a fightin' man, but aw give ye fair warnin'. If aw catch fe comin' efter wor Bell aw'll see which on us is the better chap in the use of Ns fists."

A letter was read from the Falmouth Board of Guar- dians stating that they had passed the following resalu- tion : "That, as the present system of election of Guardians is antiquated, cumbrous, and unsatisfactory in its working and opposed to modern ideas, a petition be sent to the Local Government Board urging upon them to take the necessary steps to alter the method of election to that of the ballot, and that all other Boards of Guardians be invited to support this Board in their petition. The Guardians trust that your Board will adopt this resolution,or a similar one, and so co-operate with them in endeavouring to bring about the more satisfactory mode for conducting elections of Guardians by ballot."—The Chairman asked if any member had a proposition to make.—Mr. Longton said it had been suggested that the whole question of election should be discussed, and he thought the present communication might be left over till then.

THE 81tALL-MX CASES. A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they had been informed of the outbreak of small-pox in the Union, and they forwarded a copy of the official memorandum on the steps specially requested to be taken in places where small-pox was pre- valent.—The Clerk said he had replied that the vaccina- tion officer for the district reported that he had complied with the instructions contained in the memorandum, and also that vaccination in the district was ordinarily well attended to, and everything done that could be done. _ _ _
The rest of the busiuess before the Board was of a formal character.
"IT IS THREE THOUSAND MILES
LONG."

We allude to the great Mississippi River in America. For hundreds of miles of its course it is yellow with the earth which the swift current has torn from its banks. Probably the Mississippi bears constantly in solution ground enough to make many a rich farm, though the amount is, of course, greater at times of flood. Thus, for drinking, and even for washing, the water of the Mississippi must first be purified. It is the same with anything which either for appear- ance or utility is in some way thrown opt of character. For instance, the blood in our bodies is a river. From the heart to the extremities it is of a bright red colour, but on Its return through the veins it is dark aid slug- gish. The reason is that when it starts from the heart it has jost been purified, end when it comes back it is loaded with all sorts of refuse matter it has picked up in its journey. In other words, the blood—which is only food fully digested—carries life on its red current and brings away disease and death on its dark one. Speaking of her own condition at a period about six years since, a woman writes that her skin gradually be- came first yellow and then of a saffron colour. Con- nected with this she experienced several symptoms of illness. She had more or less pain at the the sides and considerable difficulty in breathing. ger appetite, pre- viously good, began to fail, and after eating compara- tively little there was much distress in the region of the stomach. There was an attendant loss of energy, both of mind and body, and she felt tired, languid, and weak.

New we must observe that in case of natural fatigue from labour or any exertion rest is an unfailing remedy. Sleep and relaxation renew our powers. But there is a kind of fatigue which rest does not relieve—for which, the Angel of Sleep bears no healing in his wings. What vile counterfeit is this?

She adds : " I finally took to my bed and was visited by a doctor, who said my liver was wrong, and ttiat I had jaundice. He gave me medicine, but as it had no good effect he advised me to go to the hospital. As I objected to this, he said I might try a change of air and see what that would do for me. So I gave up my place and went to my borne, at Fairford, in Gloucestershire. Failing to obtain 9.ny benefit from the change, I consulted another physician, who attended me for some time, but I grew no better, Whatever I did I could not recover my strength, and my friends thought I was in a decline.

"I did not eat enough to feed a bird, and began to despair of over recovering my health. With many ups and downs in the way of feeling, and of fear and hope, I lingered along until July, 1890, when an acquaintance recommended me to try Mother Seigel's Syrup. Indeed, so much was I impressed with what was Said about this medicine that I sent my neice four miles to procure a bottle of it. After taking the centents I felt better. A weight seemed to be lifted from my chest, my relish for food returned, and by degrees I found myself in every way stronger. I will conelude by seYing that after having used two bottles more of the Syrup I was able to return to Birmingham quite well, and have had no signs of the ailment since. It is only just to mention that I feel better now than I have done for many years, and had I sootier known of Mother Seigel's Syrup I should I have avoided an amount of suffering and misery which ir it saddens me even to look hack upon:"

The lady referred to is Miss Sarah Ilawkes, of the "Lion Inn," Longmore Street, Birmingham. That yellow or saffron colour of the blood was caused by tile failure of the liver to secrete, or take away, the bile from the blood. Remaining in the blood it was carried to all parts of the body, and necessarily showed itself through the skin in the ghastly hue she names. Understand, please, that the bile, useful to help move the bowels, is a poison when in the blood. The entire malady of biliousness in all its forms is a symptom of indigestion and dyspepsia, the source of most of our aches, pains, and diseases. It is no new thing to say that the success of Mother Seigel's Syrup in reviving the torpid digestion, stimulating the liver, and thus purify. ing the blood, sets it apart from all other medicines as an article to be relied upon when the use of ordinary drugs has been followed only by ditaPpointment. The blood holds the secret of life, and this remedy keeps that ruby river tlear and clean.

A Goon Dania FoUNDAhe want of a non-alcoholic drink, which shall be refreshing and at the same time sustaining, is admitted on all sides. In our recent lead- ing article, we went very fully into the question, and during the past week we have, through the courtesy' of Mr. Lowenfeld, the proprietor of Kops Ale, had the opportunity of thoroughly investigating the mode of brewing that beverage at the Brewery, Fulham. We had never before tasted it, but now that we have done so we are bound to say that it seems to be exactly the drink which cyclers have so long felt the keen want of. It resembles bitter ale in taste and appearance, and does riot merely quench one's thirst temporarily as so many other drinks d o,but the effect lasts for an appreciable space of time. The Ale is not a mere gassy compound, but it is brewed in almost identically the same way as alcoholic beverages,and its ingredients consist,of hops, horehound, dandelion, and ginger. We are glad to hear that: the Company intends to place the Ale on sale at cycling 1 resorts, and feel confident that when Cyclers have given it a trial they will pin their faith to it.—thectm.

MR. PIERPOINT ON PAYMENT OF MEMBERS
AND MINING ROYALTIES.

Mr. RobertsPie—rpoint made a political speech at the opening of the Conservative Club Bowling Green, on Saturday. In course of it he remarked that their opponent was moving heaven and earth to get himself placed at the head of the poll; but he (Mr. Pierpoint) apprehended that he would signally fail. He had not yet had the opportunity of seeing him, but he hoped some day or other to do so, and when that time came, he would have the pleasure of being introduced to him, and would welcome him as a visitor to Warrington. (Applause.) He was told that he belonged to the Tory party, who, according to an old phrase, were in the habit of " grinding the noses of the poor," whatever that might mean. He thought he should be within the mark when he said that the men ot Warrington knew perfectly well that the Tory or Conservative party had had no inclination to "grind the noses of the poor." He had only to point out the measures which had been passed by the present Conservative Government,and the recommendation of the Government by such a man as Mr. Plimsoll, to 5140V7 that he had proof on his side. He had been accused of standing in the way of working- men getting into Parliament, by refusing to support the payment of members of Parliament. He confessed that individually, it was quite possible that the member for Warrington would very well deserve a payment for the duties he would perform in the House of Commons, but, at the same time, he was strongly of opinion that the payment of members of Parliament was contrary to the welfare of the State. (Hear, hear.) The cost of the payment, he supposed, would be some quarter of a million per annum. Besides there were plenty of com- petent men who were ready to go into Parliament to perform the duties of the offiee without any payment whatever. It was said, " You who oppose the pay- ment of membn.s of Parliament are standing in the way of working-men getting into Parliament." He was doing nothing of the sort. Suppose, now, that there was a great desire on the part of a large body of working-men to send a working-man into Parliament, it would be asking no great sacrifice for the indivi- dual working-man throughout the constituency to subscribe 23. a year to the one they wished to represent them. Suppose 4,003 working-men wanted to send a working-man to Parliament, and they were willing to subscribe 2s. a year each, an income would be obtained of £4OO a ye-r. He objected to Parliament being made a place where men might look to earning a living. It would be necessary under the circumstances to make politics a profession, it would not be the bona-fide working-man who would get in. There would, of course, be exceptions, but the mass of members, in his opinioa, would be professional politicians, who desired to make Parliament simply a means of living, and that he did not consider was as good a system as having body of men brought together from all classes—(ap- 1 plause)—who were anxious to do their best, with no payment, for the good of the community. At the risk of wearying them he would touch upon one more ques- tion. A great deal was being talked—and he said something about it the other night at La chford—con- corning Mining Royalties. He had been taken to task be- cause he did not express a willingness to abolish mining royalties. England was compared with other countries,and great landlords were referred to as the owners of mining royalties. The old English law concerning the possession of land, whether it was a large piece of land, a large estate, or a little plot of half an acre, was that everything above the land and everything below belonged to the owner of the scil. Suppose a man had bought out of his savings a couple of acres of land, and there was coal underneath, was the State to deprive him of that coal for ' the benefit of one class of men; or, if there was iron ore, was he to be deprived of it, because they must remem- ber that if they took what was the property of the large landlord they would have to take the property of the small one? In those cases no royalty was paid, as a rule because the rights had been bought out and out for a capital sum paid down; in the case of large estates it often happened that a man worked the minerals himself. In that ease he paid himself a royalty ; on the other hand, a man might let it off in royalties to a coal owner, who gathered the coal, paying him so much per ton or an acre, but the land had been valuable in consequence of the coal being underneath all the time, and was less ' valuable when the coal was taken out by a great deal. Assume for a moment that the State had a right to con- fiscate the property of the great and of the small, and to seize what was beneath the surface : What would be the result? Did they suppose that when confiscation was given in the confiscation of the coal and the iron ore the community would • not share in it ? Were the iron workers and the coal workers to benefit alone by the confiscation? It confiscation was to be allowed, all would want their thare—the butcher, the baker, and the candlestick maker, and every other man. They would all want a share. If, on the other hand, they were to say that the State should seize upon these, and compensate the owners, who was going to pay the com- pensation money? The community would have to pay it, and the butchers, bakers, and candlestick makers would all have to pay their share. Would they pay for the benefit of one particular class of men ? Certainly not. They would demand that the matter should be treated fairly between man and man. (Ap- plause.) As to the question between France and Bel- gium, which has been referred to, the law was different. Of course when a man owned property he owned it subject to the law of the State in which it was, and when a man bought apiece of property in France, or in Belgium, he bought it subject to the fact that he was , not the owner of everything beneath the surface. The mining laws in America were the same as the mining : laws in Eneland, namely, that the Americans had the same laws as we had. He had ventured to make these remarks in order that he might make it a little clearer to them why he was not in favour of what was broadly and airily called "the abolition of mining royalties."

div.head: WARRINGTOA.'CPNWST,,I
div.p: THE WARRINGTOA.'CPNWST,,I
THE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE'S ANSWERS TO RAILWAY SAVANTS.

Mr. Robert Pierpoiut bes at length sent a reply to the questions Sublititted to him on behalf of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, of which Mr. H. Ogden, of Collings-st., is the secretary of the local branch, and to him the replies were addressed. They read as follows : Quesrioe I.—" A maximum working day of ten hours, with six days to the week, for all railway employes, such hours to be regulated and enforced by the Board of Trade, the necessary powersibeing obtained for that purpose from Parliament." Answer: "The questions which you put before me on behalf a the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servant e are of such importance as, I think, to justify full consideration, weich you will please accept as an apology for the late- ness of my reply. While lam of opinion that, as a gen- eral rule, al° hours' working day on a railway is long enough, still I think Major Marindin (one of the Beard of Trade Inspectors) is right in saying Owing to the enormous variety of circumstances under which rail- way servants :work, it would be utterly impossible to lay down a hard and fast rule as to the hours of work.' Further, I believe that et would be contrary to the in- terests of the men that they should be forbidden by law to work overtime if they choose to do so. Take the case of a man who has been out of work for a few weeks, and has run into debt. It would, in my opinion, be very hard upon him that he should not be permitted to make up his lost time. As to the hard and fast rule, am Ito suppose that you believe that, whereas a day ,of eight hours is probably quite long enoegli for the driver of an express train, three hours more would be too much for a porter at a little wayside station ; that the man in charge of a bully signal box has no greater strain on his attention than the man in charge of one where few trains pass, or that men in charge of a train vrhice has been delayed are to be compelled by statute to leave their train on the line, wherever it happens to be, when their ten hours are up?" QUESTION 2—" An effective supervision • over the working of all railways, which shall include periodical inspection by qualified and practical sub-inspectors, who shall act under the existing Board of Trade inspec- tork:"—Answer "If the present inspection by the Board of Trade is insufficient, most certainly there should be more inspectors, or sub-inspectors." QUESTION 3.—" Board of Trade inquiries to be held in all CUPS of serious accidents to employee where such occur in the movement of vehicles, and not, as now, to be mainly confined to accidents in which public safety is directly involved."—Answer : "I quite agree with the suggestion that there should be Board of Trade in- quiries into all cases of serious accidents to railway workmen, including those which occur to shunters and platelayers." Questiote 4.—" Railway companies to be compelled to provide self-acting coupling appliances for shunters and effective protection for platelayers when working on the permanent way during the course of public traffic, and that wherever possible automatic fog signalling be sub- stituted for the present system." Answer: "As far as I have been able to ascertain, there has not yet been any effective self-acting coupler invented. If there were one I have no doubt that the railway companies would be very eager to adopt it. I cannot see that there any necessity for legislating about an invention not yet made with a view of compelling directors to do that which (granted the invention) they would be quite willing to do of their own accord. I beg to remind yoir that the adoption of self-acting couplers would entail the dis- missal of thousands of Shunter, whose services would be no longer required. I think that a company should be obliged to provide effective protection for plate-layers, and that, whenever possible, automatic fog-signalling, if effective, should be used." Quesnoe 5.—" Certificates of competency, On the lines laid down in the measure commonly known as the Engineman's Certificate Bill, to be held by all engine drivers, without which it shall be illegal for anyone to take charge of an engine. The Board of Trade to grant the certificates, which shall be altogether independent of the companies." Answer: "As to the proposal that no man shall be allowed to drive an engine who is not provided with a certificate of competency from the Board of Trade, not having any reason to doubt that practically all the engine drivers now employed are per- fectly competent men, I see no necessity for their hav- ing certificates to prove that which, as I take it, is already proved by the very responsible positions which they hold, and by the exceeding rarity of accidents occurring through engine drivers' faults. Your suggestion appears to amount to this that there is at present a proportion of incompetent men amongst the engine drivers sufficient to justify an ex- amination by the Board of Trade. I cannot agree with this suggestion that there is any appreciable proportion. I would point out to you that, in view of the liability far heavy damages, setting aside other considerations, it is of the greatest importance to the railway companies that they should employ only the best men." Queseme B.—" Au Employers Liability Act, on the lines of the Bill moduced by Mr. T. Burt, M.P., in which the unjustl doctrine of common employment shall have no place, and contracting out to be made illegal. The amount which may be claimed shall he unlimited, as in ordinary common law while the period for giving notice of intention to proceed under the Act shall be extended to six months." Answer: I should be inclined to support an Employers • Liability Bill abolishing the doctrine of common employment, but I am not inclined to think that =trading out should be illegal, because I think that such a provision would be an invasion of the right of freq conteact, and against the interests of the men. I understand that it is the custom now on most, if not on all lines, where men con- tract out of the Act, for a sum of about Bd. per week to be set aside from the wages for insurance and provident funds, &c., and that the companies add to the amount thus saved a like or nearly like amount. For example, I the Manchester Sheffield. and Lincolnshire subscribe to to these funds from £4,000 to £5,000, the London and North-Western abogt £24.000, and the Midland about £22,000 a year. It is probable that in the event of con- tracting out being made illegal these heavy sums of money would be no longer subscribed. I approve of the suggestion that claims made by the men should be un- limited, and that the time for giving notice of intention to claim should be extended considerably." _

div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. In the absence of Mr. Mclntyre, who was indisposed thrcugh a bronchial attack, Mr. J. Knowles presided, and there were present—Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Whitlow, H. E. Hey- wood, J. M. Williams, P. Hall, J. Brandreth, J. Weir, A. Greenway, J. Ashton (clerk), G. div.head: FRODSLIAM WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: FRODSLIAM WATER SUPPLY.

The Parochial Committee of Frodsham held a meeting on the 20th May, when the Clerk read a letter from Messrs. Morrell and Son with respect to the land required for the proposed scheme of water supply for Frodsham, when, on the motion of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Davies, it was resolved that the agreement be accepted in the terms altered and completed. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Davies, that Messrs. Timmins, engineers, of Runcorn, be in- formed that the land and way leaves required for carry- ing out the scheme of water supply submitted by them had been arranged for at a cost,exclusive of legal charges and compensation to tenants, of £350, and that they be requested to reconsider their estimate of the cost of the scheme and submit the same for the con- sideration of the Committee.—At a subsequent meet- ing of the Committee held on the 27th May, Messrs. ! Timmins submitted an estimate and details for supply- ing portions of the township of Frodsham with water. Pumping stations with artesian well and boring with pumping powers capable of raising 5,000 gallons per hour 250 feet,and provision for duplicate machinery, brick engine house, reducing valve brick building to supply west end of Frodsham, exclusive of mains £972 103. 101 ; covered brick reservoir of 125,000 gallons capacity £650; stand pipes, fine hydrant, pair of relief valves £ll5 ss. ; pumping and distribution mains £1,162 43. 23. ; preparation of plan and supervisbn during constructionof work £100; land and way leave, law charges and compensation to tenants £75 ; add 10 per cent, for contingencies £3,767 53. It was resolved that Messrs. Timmins's scheme and plans be approved and adopted and that the central authority be requested to forward the plans, report, and estimates to the Local Government Board for their approval ; also that the central authority be requested to make application to the Local Government Board fur their Lordships' sanc- tion to a loan of £3,800 for carrying out the proposed scheme for a water supply to the township of Frodsham. —Mr. Heywood moved the adoption of the minutes, and that the Rural Sanitary Authority act as requested. —Mr. Aaron seconded the motion.—Mr. Brandreth remarked that the rateable value of Frodsham was £14.000, but Mr. Heywood said the cost of this scheme would not fall upon the whole of the township. The minutes were approved.

Last time they heard anything about it, it was in operation, but they had no intimation that it had been completed success- fully or otherwise.—Mr. Farrington said the sub-agent of the estate told him that they were waiting for Mr. White, the agent, who had been ill, to fix where the engine, &c., should be placed. They had got a tank,"&c., on the ground, but no attempt was made to start opera- tions.—Mr. Aaron said this matter had bom going on for two years, and it was postponed time after time. He therefore proposed that the clerk write to headquarters. This was seconded and carried.

At tbefortnightly meeting held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday, Sir. J. Knowles presided in the .absence of the Chairman, through indisposition,and there were present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. div.head: PROPOSED TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: PROPOSED TRIENNIAL ELECTIONS.

With respect to the proposal to hold the election of Guardians triennially, the Local Government Board wrote that they were unable to express any opinion as to tbe probable cost of a poll of owners and ratapayera of the Runcorn Union on the subject of the suggested alteration of the period of service of Guardians of the Union. At the same time there was enclosed copy of an order issued by the Board to the Guardians of Falmouth Union which would show the nature of the proceedings in connection with such a poll, and to state that the Board had recently issued orders directing the triennial election of Guardians in the following Unions, viz. Watford, Grimsby, Falmouth, Cheltenham, Wisbech, Burtdertand, Auckland,Holtreaeh,Llandilo Fawr, Ipswich, and Llanelly. The Board suggested that some informa- tion as to cost might probably be obtained by communi- cating with the Clerks to the Guardians of the Unions named.—The Clerk said he had made a rough cal- culation, and he estimated that a poll would cost .£l5O were it conducted on the same scale as an election of Guardians„—Mr. Heywood said he would postpone the motion of which he had given notice until the clerk communicated with the Unions mentioned in the letter and obtained fuller information as to the ad- vantages of havimg triennial electors instead of annual. After the first expense there would be a saving of £1.3 63. Bd. per year on the returning officers' fees ; besides there would be the saving of the cost of the contested elections two years out ot three. The clerk to the Union strongly recommended triennial elections • although it would be against himself financially, and the clerk to the Warrington Union had informed him (Mr. Heywood) that the system had answered very well in the Warring- ton Union. They got better men for the work, because they were not subject to constant change.—The Clerk said he w 9uid obtain further information on the subject.

div.head: 'THE BALLOT WANTED.
div.p: 'THE BALLOT WANTED.

A letter was re;cl.-f-r;TiTtleFalmouth Union asking the Guardians to support a petition they had forwarded to the Local Governraent Board asking for the ballot to be introduced into elections of Guardians.—Mr. Taylor said he should he very glad to see the ballot introduced. The present mode was most unsatisfactory,and he hoped the Board would do all in their power to get the law altered. (Hear, hear.) The other members present agreed, and Mr. Williams gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that a petition be sent to the Local Government Board on the subject.

div.head: DEFAULTING TOWNSWIPS.
div.p: DEFAULTING TOWNSWIPS.

In reply to Mr. Aaran, Mr. Bra mireth said the town- ships which had not yet paid their calls were :—Acton Grange, Antrobus, Bartington, Budworth, Clipton, Crowley, Frodsham, Halton, Helsby, Kingsley, Kings- wood, Norley, Preston-o'-th'-liill, Sutton, and Whitley Superior. Those townships which had paid were Alvan- ley, Appleton, Aston, Aston Grange, Da.resbury,Dutton, Frodsham Lordship, Flalton, Keckwick, Manley, Moore, Newton-by-Dareskury, Newton-by-Frodsham, Norton, Runcorn, Seven Oaks, Stockham, Stretton, Walton In- ferior Walton Superior, Whitley Inferior, and Weston.— Mr. In- ferior, said it was many years since calls were so well paid, so that the action of the Board on the last occasion had done good.

div.head: " EAWR OWD STATION MESTER."
div.p: " EAWR OWD STATION MESTER."

AW've travelt mony a theawsand miles, An' met aw sooarts an' sizes, Fro them ez 'wasn't up to mitch, To thoose ez turn't eawt prizes. But noan like him ez acts on ins Just like a warmin' plaster; Woze aiquil yo'd be pushed to find— Eawr own owd Station-Mester. It's spend to hear his cheery vice Gie one an' aw "Good inornin' " ; Not knucklin' deawn to th'llpper Ten, Nor th' other classes scornin'. Yo'at hunt fro Lunnnn to Chowbent— 'Fro Tilsley Bongs to Chester— But yole find never one to byet Eawr own owd Station Mester. Theer at his post, fro morn to fleet, Yole alias see him workin' ; Nosiooart o' weather frickens him- -He's noan the mon fez shirkin. Rain, hail, or snow,—or cosid winds blow,— ' Nor'-easter or sow'-wester— aw the same—true to his time— Yole find eawr Station Mester. Smart ez a sojer on parade, He's theer at strict attention; An' one smaw fible that he hex. Aw'll tek French leave to mention. Them lovely &ewers ! but, bless yer sowl, They ne'er cost him a tester: For lovin' bonds fro' far and wide, Bring um to th' Station Mester An' wen is duty's done fez th' day, O'er pipe an' glass' yo' meet him; If yo're like me, yo'le jump at th' chance To shake his bond, an' greet him. He's full o' fun an' divilment,— No spite in him con fester; But theer he is, ez true ez steel,— Bawr own owd Station Mester Owd mon f wen uz two hop the twig, An' fro' this world we hook it, So wheer theaw goes, aw'll be content To tak' my seat an' book it. An' if ther shud be railway trains To bother an' to pester; Aw'll be quite satisfied, owd lad, If theawet eawr Station Mester! TIM 0' PEGS. Nyowton, God bless o'. June Ist, 1892.
THE CHURCH DIFFERENCES AT BURTON WOOD. EXTRAORDINARY APPEAL

The parishioners of Burtonwood Church, near St. Helens, who have recently had aotne. " differencet " with their new vicar, the Rev. A. Id. Mitchell, and to which frequent references have been made, have been considerably interested in an appeal for contri butions which appeared in a recent issue of a church periodical. The " appeal " was as follows : Church in Lancashire. Churchmen to the rescue. Splendid opportunity for establishing Church principles in a benighted quarter of Lancashire. Burtonwood, in , the diocese of Liverpool, is in immediate need of help from all loyal Churchmen. A stronghold of Roman- ism and dissent. People prejudiced ; some hos- tile; vicar harassed. Wanted immediately, £5OO to complete vicarage fund. (£BOO already secured; no house to be had in parish ; vicar has to walk seven miles to daily offices); £5OO to build parochial room (no room of any kind available, popu- lation over 1,600; many colliers); £250 to put church r and churchyard in decent repair ; £l5O a year towards supporting a curate, mission nurse, and Church Army officer (vicar single-handed, parish contains three ham- lets, and covers area of six square miles). Work done in three months: Church made open, daily prayers established, early and saints' day celebrations instituted, a weekly offering introduced, sanctuary made comely, , Church Army set to work. Contributions to be for- warded to the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Burtonwood, Newton-le-Willows with the least possible delay. To ithe help of the Lord against the mighty." The worshippers who attended the church on Sunday noticed some additional " improvements " or " innovia- tions " in the fittings of the chancel and communion. Two handsomely carved old oak chairs, which it is understood had done duty in the old couatry church for many years, had been replaced by plain wooden seats; while a small prayer desk had been erected in the com- munion and a brass altar desk placed on the credence table. Hitherto the sacramental vessels in use were of a massive, plain silver description, but for these were substinited two glass Vessels with. silver crosses at the top. Not only had these visible changes been made, but in commencing, his sermon,- the vicar, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, intimated that be had decided to make some slight alterations in the services. He explained that it was his intention to shorten the ordinary service by leaving out certain prayers which occurred in die office- for morning prayer, and again in the communion.- He did not think it nec- essary that such prayers should be repeated after once being given, and lie wonld also emit one hymn. Ho remarked that it had been the cusioni, after the prayer on the presentation of the alms, to have a pluse in the service while the organ struck up a voluntary and allowed those who wished to depart to do so. He band that this was a wronl comae to adopt, and he proposed that there shquld be no break in the service at all. He asked WI -.9 _ear brothers and sist,is to stay for the com- munion, but if they imist sway they could leave the church whilst he read the exhortation. This concluded
'NgSTd T;teliaa

his announcements, and in accordance therewith tla. , parishioners left. the church whilst the exhortation was ' being read. It is stated that there were extremely few remaining to the communiAn service. The vicar has recently discontinued using the black stole whilst con- ducting the service, and has substituted a white silk gown with gold fringe and crosses.

div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEER ENCAMPMENT.
div.p: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEER ENCAMP- MENT.

On Tuesday afternoon, a contingent of ten of thi Warrington Volunteers proceeded, with Captain Baynes in command, by the London and North— Western Railway Co.'s line to Conway, which is to be the :•cene of the encampment of the battalion this year. On Wednesday morning a party of 16 men, followed, and to-day (Saturday) the remainder of the battalion will go into camp. Toe Warrington battalion will fall in at half-past seven to-night at the Drill Hail and will leave by train about an hour later, for Conway, which they will reach about 11 eclock.

Altogether it is honed that 4,000 men will be ,present from the various battalions. General Thackwell, C. 8., will be in command, and the troops taking part in the training will be the Ist, 2nd, and 3rd Battalions Lana.- shire Fuailiers the iVarrington Volunteers, Ist Battalion ' (P. W. V.) South Lancashire Regiment ; and the 4th and sth Battalions, Cheshire Regiment. It is pointed out that if 300 members of the Battalion encamp the days of coming into and leaving camp are included in the pay, and it is to be hoped that as mahy of our local defenders as can make it convenient will put in an appearance at camp. The camp will break tip soon after dinner next Saturday. The Warringtrin battalion will be inspected at Warrington on July 23rd, by Colonel fwentyman. The ground chosen will probably be a field at Arpley be- longing to Captain and Quartermaster Hutchinson.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW ASSEMBLY ROOM
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW ASSEMBLY ROOM

FOR WARRINGTON. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committes which was held on Monday afternoon, the sub. Committee which had been appointed to consider a scheme on constructing public offices and works, submitted its report. As stated last week, the sub-Committee's conclusion as to a Public Hall was that the Corporation had not power to provide on Assembly Hall, unless it were in conjunction with build- ings used for municipal purposes. Councillor H. lt,berts objected to the report of the sub-Committee and con- tended that they had no authority to report on a public Hall, as it was outside their instructions. He was sup- ported in this view by Councillors Blackhu:st and Sbaw-Green. Alderman Chand'ey took offence at the objection which had been raised, and an altercation ensued between him and Councillor Roberts. A long discussion followed, and some of the speakers suggested that Warrington was badly off for a Corn Exchange, and that, as the present Market Hall was practically useless, it might be converted into a Corn Exchange, with a large room and offices, either over or 11 on the basement story ; which might be used either for I public meetings or concerts and such like entertain- ments. The discussion ended by the unanimous passing of a resolution that the Borough Surveyor be requested to go into the question of the suggested conversion, and to report generally and fully to the committee forthwith, as to the feasibility and desirability of dealing with the present Market Hall in the way proposed. With regard to the general scheme for concentrating offices and works on some such plan as originally pro- posed by Councillor R. T. Fairclough, the conclusion come to was that it would be a very large undertaking and would involve a larger expenditure than the Cor- poration were prepared to undergo at the present time.
THE NEW WESLEYAN SUNDAY scnona
AT SANKEY BRIDGES.

On Tuesday evening, what may be termed the first of a series of opening services in connection with the above schools was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Sankey Bridges, The formal opening of the new schools will take place in July, when Dr. Woods of Southport will conduct the services. The service on Tuesday was conducted by the well. known Wesleyan minister and temperance orator —the Rev. Charles Garrett, of Liverpool. The schools which are now almost completed have been in the hands of Mr. John Longshaw, builder, the plans being tarnished by Mr. Percy Silcock, archi- tect, Egypt-st., and it may safely be predicted that the accommodation will meet the requirements of the district for many years to come. The service was attended by a large congregation. Special hymns were sung by the children of the school,and choir to the number of about 100, under tire eble conductorship of Mr. Walter Brough. A spevial feature was the orchestral accompaniments, assisted by Mr. Thomas Brough on the harmonium. The Rev. Charles Garrett took his text from Hebrews, 13th chapter, sth verse. " Let your conversation be without covetousness, and be content with such things as you have, for he hath said I will never leave thee." In the course of his remarks, he said covetousness was an almost universally besetting sin. It was not the sin of the rich alone, nor alone that of the poor. It did not follow that because a man had very little, he was net covetous. He might have an earnest desire to be rich, and to possess some of those things which others enjoyed. Covetousness was also a most subtle sin. There were some sins they could deal with, but what could they do with covetousness ? It was out of sight. They could tell whether a man was a drunkard, but they could not tell whether he was covetous, and he had never heard of a man bemg expelled from the church because be was covetous. Yet they were told that covetousness shut a man out of the Kingdom. The more a covetous man had the more he wasted, and there were some men who would coin blood out of those nearest and dearest to them. There was a second part, and that was the duty of being content with such things as we had. It did not mean that we were not to improve ourselves, No! young men, were perfectly right in trying to improve their position if they could; and if they had get to the first rung in the ladder let them go on. It did not mean, either, that we were not to be economical, for we knew that Christ disap- proved o: waste. At the conclusion .of his sermon, which was listened to with great attenben, im appealing for a liberal response at the collection, the rev, gentle- man said the friends at Sankey Bridges had done a noble work. He had to preach against covetousness, or he would have coveted the new school as well as the chapel. He alluded to the joy it would be to them in tpe future to think that they helped to put that room up. He hoped the blessing of God would still attend their efforts, A collection was then taken, and after a hymn had been sung and the Benediction pronounced, the service con. duded.

div.head: LEAMINGTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE LEAMINGTON TRAGEDY.

William Ernest Grearex, 37, of St. John's Wood, London was on Wednesday charged at the Leamington Police &int with murdering his father, James Frederick Greatrea. The prisoner, who is a thick-set man of average height, was well dressed, and seemed totally indifferent. Ho was not represented by a solicitor. Evidence was given to the effect that he shot his father twice with a revolver, remarking "You have what you deserve, and I have what I want." He said to the con- stable who arrested him, "It's all right, officer; here you are; I did it," and handed the revolver, which was ' loaded in four chambers, to the constable. The prisoner was remanded pending Friday's inquest. He eats well, ' slept soundly, and continu.s apparently extremely cheerful. The police fear that he will commit suicide, as he states that he intended to shoot himAelf, but his courage failed. A constable is always with him, to whom he chats. It is stated that his relatives, believing his mind affected, had contemplated putting him under restraint..

div.head: LIVERPOOL PUBLICANS AND FEMALE
div.p: LIVERPOOL PUBLICANS AND FEMALE
CUSTOMERS.
IMPORTANT DECISION IN THEL QUEEN'S BENCH.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Thursday, before Baron Pollock and Justice Vaughan Williams,' the case of Sharp v. Hughes raised an important point under the Licensing Acts. It was an appeal by Sharp, landlord of a public-house at Liverpool, against a decision of the quarter Session justices refusing to renew appellant's license on the ground that the house had been unsatis- factorily conducted, and WAS a resort of improper females. Council for the appellant contended it wai I not shown that appellant had allowed the women to remain on the premises lonv-r than was necessary for purposes of obtaining refreshment, or that they resorted to the place for the purposes of their calling. Their lordships, however, held that the justices clearly had discretion to refuse the licence without any misconduct, but as they did not wish it to go forth that they con- sidered the frequenting of a house by these women for the purposes of obtaining refreshment was a sufficient cause for refusing the license the case must go back to be restated with instructions that the ground tor refus- ing the license be snore fully set out.

MITCHELL does not succeed in raking in the shekels, it is not because he is I,ll_et "a beggar to beg." Indeed, the ordinary 'gging,-letter writer isn't in it.
