STONE has accepted tho recent voting at the polls as an intimation that the London question must be one of the earliest to be dealt with in the new Parliament, after the granting of Home Rule to Ireland. It must be remembered that the issue at stake affects a population of four millions—almost as large as the population of the whole of Ireland ; and that no just reason can be given for with- holding the common rights of citizenship. There is, it is true, a Corporation of the city of London ; but it controls but a fraction of London proper; and it is essentially Tory because it is based on the privileges of the classes. It has an electorate, as Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out, of 31,700 of whom from 7,000 to 8,000 are livery men. What this means will be best understood when it is stated tha t nearly 6,000 of these livery nlen are " entirely devoid of the householding qualification." In contrast to this is another Pert of London—St. Georges-in-the-East—with a Populationof 48,000, while of those 3,600 only are voters. There ought to be at least double the number of electors; and there will be, when, along With the reform of London, there is a reform of the registration laws. But London suffers chiefly through a multipli- city of overlapping authorities. The City Cor- poration has control over a relatively small area, While other portions of the metropolis are gov- erned, after a fashion, by twenty-three " select ' vestries, and fifteen district boards. What is Deeded is unification and consolidation of authori- ties, offices, and duties, with the result that there, Will be greater economy and better management. It will follow too, that a more capable body of men Will take part in the government of London, when London is governed as a whole. But what need is !here to argue the question ? T o best argument 18, after all, to be found in the fa..l-, that local self- government has been tried for a generation in every great centre, except Loulon, and it has not been found wanting.

Several letters and other communications— some of them received late—are crowded out.

Parr's Banking Company, Limited,'has effected another amalgamation. This time it is absorbing the Alliance Bank, Limited, London. The extra foothold which will thus be gained in the metro- polis will doubtless tend to strengthen and develop an already remarkably prosperous Com- pany. It is a feather in the cap of Warrington to be the centre of such an institution.

The Durham strike has been brought to an end through the mediation of the Bishop of Durham. It has been a case of both sides conceding some- thing. The men have consented to accept a re- duction of 10 per cent., but tile coalowners sought a reduction of 13i per cent. In future, disputes are to be settled by a Board of Concilation. The Bishop is to be congratulated on the success of his intervention. " All's well that ends well."

The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority are taking the right course in directing the attention of the Medical Officer of Health to the nuisance caused at Stockton Heath arising from the deposit of night-soil and other offensive matter in a dis- used sand-hole. In time the sand-hole will be filled up, and built upon, with the prospect of the houses erected on this " made ' land proving insanitary, and possibly becoming fever dens.

At last gr. Robert Pierpoint, the Tory candi- date for Warrington, who is very busy doing no- thing, has found time to reply to the questions put to him by the Railway Servants. It will be seen from his replies that he sits on the fence, ready as circumstances may servo to jump down on either side. His laboured and indefinite answers are in striking contrast to the replies furnished several weeks ago by Dr. Houston : and railway men will be in no doubt as to which candidate will best serve them.

It is due to Mr. Pierpoint to say that he is de- finite enough on one point, and that is that he is not in favour of payment of members. But what is the object of paying members Is it not to give poor men an equal chance with rich in repre- senting their class in Parliament ? And if that be so, does it not follow that Mr. Pierpoint refuses to deal justly with the very men upon whose votes he depends to be returned to Parliament ?

Let working-men, Tory working-men if you like, reason this out; and then ask themselves if it is fair that, for the matter of a quarter of a mil- lion a year, a barrier shopld be kept up to prevent the best amongst them having a seat in the House of Commons ? The labourer is worthy of his hire whether in the House or out of it ; and, if contin- ental States can afford to pay members, England can and should afford.

The Queen has made a present of a white goat to the 2nd V.B. Royal Welsh Fusiliers; and the battalion aie mightily pleased with the gift. There is a story told of a Spanish Ambassador who met with small favour from the court to which he was accredited, because of his juvenile appearance. The King even openly referred to him as beard- less, upon which the proud Spaniard said the monarch he represented would have sent a goat had he known it was a beard that was required. What of the Welsh goat? Has it got a beard?

It is a noteworthy and satisfactory sign of the times that even Tory candidates are expressing themselves in favour of peace principles and arbi- tration in the case of disputes with other nations. It is to the credit of the Government of the United States that they have expressed them- selves as willing to conclude a treaty with any nation to refer all disputes which may arise to arbitration. Lord Salisbury, however, makes no sign : he has something of the Jingo in him. At the annual meeting, on Monday, of the Interna- tional Arbitration and Peace Association strong dissatisfaction was expressed that the Prime Minister had taken no steps to meet the practical offer of the United States.

Widnes is ahead of London in one respect ; it is now possessed of full powers of local self-govern- ment, having received its charter of incorporation on Monday last. The inhabitants are to be con- gratulated upon the development of the town. It has grown rapidly,. despite the ever-present perfume which isnot that of eau de Cologne. By- the-bye, it is odd, isn't it ? that Cologne should stand, so to speak, for foul smells as well as sweet ones. This is what Coleridge had to say of it : I counted two and seventy stenches, All well defined and several stinks. The river Rhine it is well-known Doth wash the city of Cologne ; But tell me, nymphs ! What power divine Shall henceforth wash the river Rhine ?

There seems to have been an extraordinary conflict of evidence in the case heard at Daresbury, on Tuesday, with regard to the alleged cruelty to a girl. Dr. Joseph swore to noticing, on Saturday, four contused wounds on the left side of the girl's back • while Dr. Cannell, who made an examination on Monday, not only said he found no marks; but added that he "did not believe any doctor could have found four contused wounds on the girl." Such a reflection by one professional man on the evidence of another is fortunately very unusual in this cOuntry. The days of duelling are over, or the end of the cross-examination would have been "crossed swords," or "coffee and pistols." Under the circumstances, we presume it will simply have to be said of the two medical men—" They never speak as they pass by."

"The Christian World" says:—" A good story was told at the Disestablishment Conference re- cently held at Carmarthen. One of the speakers instanced a case of a branch of the Church of Eng- land in a rural district in Wales, the attendants at which were limited to the vicar and the sexton. On a certain Sunday, half the congregation was prostrated with the influenza, but the service was held as usual, and the vicar discoursed laboriously on 'The Church Invisible.'" Something similar has happened nearer home. One morning this week, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, of Burtonwood, had a service of prayer; and had the place to him- self, until a Pressman looked in, on the hunt for an inter View with the reverend gentleman.

The " Conservative " whose little trick we exposed last week, which consisted in comparing the results of twelve years of Tory administration with six years of Liberal rule, has attempted to defend himself,in our Tory contemporary,by assert- ing that "two like periods were submitted." If he remembers what he has written, he must know that he is not telling the truth. We have his communication before us, and we repeat that it is what we described it—a comparison of twelve years of Tory against six years of Liberal adminis- tration. If there is any Tory reader who may have a doubt as to where the truth lies, he can be shown " Conservative's " letter on applying at the office of this journal.

But " Conservative " publicly convicts himself in Wednesdays" Observer," for he gives what he calls " Lists of measures passed solely or mainly in the interests of the working classes from 188.6 to 1891." What an absurd comparison seeing that the Liberals have not been in office since 1886 ! He, however, gives 10 Liberal measures, after making out a list of Tory measures ; but, according to his showing, they were all passed between from 1880 to 1884. How then can they be said to come under the head of measures passed" from 1886 to 1891 P" Really if "Con- servative " thinks he can gull Conservatives by such a mass of self-contradiction, he must have a lower opinion of their intelligence than even we ourselves have.

div.p: ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.

At Itnneorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Major Haztehurst and Mn Jame Handley, Thomas Massey, of Warrington, was summoned for cruelly illtreatino•" a horse. P.C. Petting,ale stated that at 11 a.m. on the 17th inst., he saw the defendant in charge of acob at- tached to a lurry laden with metals, going up Bridge- st., and the defendant was whipping it. He did this for some time until opposite the big lamp, where he stopped the animal, and then thrashed it again. The Constable interfered, and defendant obtained a chain horse to assist with the load.—This statement was corroborated. —The defendant said he struck the horse once. He was cracking the whip and the Constable thought he was striking the horse. It was an entire horse, and if he did not master it it would kill somebody. George Howard, the defendant's employer, said he examined the horse when he got home, and there were no marks whatever. There was only 24cwt. on the lurry, and it was able to draw a much heavier load. A fine of 2s. and costs, IBs.,was imposed. ' On Thursday afternoon, an inquest was held by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, on the body of Samuel Adams, a foreman quarryman, who resided in , Tay- -1 ' or-st. Runcorn, and died in the Ship Canal Hospi- tal at Latchford, on Monday, from the effects of injuries received while pursuing his work. He was foreman of a gang of men who were working in the Weston Quarries, and were removing pieces of loose rock, and he was standing on the edge of a ledge leaning on hie crowbar when a loose piece of rock fell, knocking away the crowbar, and Adams fell on to a ledge 27 feet below. He lighted on his feet, but before he had time to recover himself a piece of ro,:k weighing two cwt. fell from above and crushed him, and he received such shocking in- juries that death resulted soon afterwards. The jury returned a verdict that he had met with his death accidentally. Cricketing GoorIs.—GARLAND, Sports' Warehouse, War- rington.

div.head: BLASTING ACCIDRNT AT A COLLIERY. _ _
div.p: BLASTING ACCIDRNT AT A COLLIERY. _ _

On Tuesday morning a serious accident occurrel at the Collins Green Colliery, near St. Helens, by which two men—John Moore, collier, of Watery- lane, Sutton, and his half-brother, Thomas M'Glue, drawer, of Mercer'scottages,Burtonwood—received horrible injuries. It appears that on the previous night the two men, who worked together, had drilled holes in the face of the coal ready for the insertion of the blasting cartridges. In ramming home one of the shots the fuse was broken, and the charge could not be extracted or the shot fired. The men were told to make another hole on Tuesday morning, and they were doing this when the charge left in from the previous night suddenly exploded. It blew off right in the faces of the two men, both of whom were shockingly burned and injured about the head, arms, and body. They were removed to their homes as early as possible and medical assis- tance was obtained. UMBRELLAS nitcovintEh.-7. and W. furrow, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

"BT AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The presentation of prizes to the successful students at Runcorn Evening Classes last week end gave Mr. James Pritchard, the Chairman of the School Board, an opportunity to make a few appro- priate remarks on the subject of education. The Bcrlrd had commenced the class with some misgiv- ings, but the success which had attended the two sessions have agreeably surprised the members of the Board. Not only was the number, of students large, but the success achieved at the examinations was highly satisfactory, and the report ot 11.31. Inspector, though brief, was eminently gratifying. It read "This school is ably and intelligently con- ducted and is doing h good work." -Mr. Pritchard expressed the hope that the young people would conac forward in increased numbers and also take advantage of the Science and Art classes held in the school. By obtaining education suitable for the , occupations in which they were engaged, they would be better able to perform their work which would become not an irksome task but a pleasure, and they would be so improved intellectually that it would be in their power to infuse a brightness and joy into their surroundings which had perhaps been previously wanting. •

Now there are some people who look upon the proposed Technical Institute through most pessi- mistic spectacles, and some even go so far to pre- dict that it will fail to attract students in any large numbers. Of course it cannot be said that the science and art classes conducted this winter have been an unqualified success, especially so far as the members presented for examination are con- cerned, but it must be remembered that they were somewhat hurriedly arranged, and that it is a ques- tion of years before a science school gets thoroughly established, and its advantages are estimated at their true value. The evening classes will be an admirable training ground for the more advanced ' subjects of the Technical Institute, and if the Board of Commissioners will at once take steps for constructing the building they will earn the gratitude of this and future generations. The appeal for subscriptions appears to have fallen very flat: it certainly was not a very inspiring document; and lam afraid there will be no practi- cal response. So far as I can learn, Mr. Philip Speakman is the only local gentleman who has made any promise, and it is surprising that more have not followed his excellent example. However notwithstanding the dearth of voluntary offerings Runcorn ought to have its technical school, and it is to be hoped that the Commissioners will not hesitate to provide it out of the rates if no ether way is open.

Mr. Cunnab, the master of Dutton Workhouse has decided upon Blackpool as the place where the workhouse children shall spend a happy day in the near future. It is estimated that the trip will cost at least £l5, and the master's appeal for subscrip- tions met with a generous reply from a number of gentlemen in the Union, the sum of ..£l2 Bs. being raised. The name of Mr. G. Whiteley, the Conser- vative candidate for Northwich Division, appeared amongst the subscribers. In order to make up the difference the hat was sent round at the Guardians' meeting on Tuesday, with gratifying results.

The annual meeting of the Board of Commissioners is due to take place this month, and that interest- ing event, the election of a Chairman, is the chief item on the agenda. For some years past it has been the rule to make the selection by order of seniority,so that in the course of time each member would fill the presidential chair, without regard to his ability or suitability. Now, I don't know whose " turn" it is on the present occasion, but in my opinion the rule is a pernicious one; and ought to be broken. And the present time offers a favour- able opportunity for making a "new departure." Amongst the members is one who, by his own energy, perseverance, and ability has risen from the lowest rung of the ladder to a position of power and responsibility in a great firm, to whose instrumentality the ratepayers, in a great measure, owe the now popular Victoria-road, and who, in other departments of the town's business, since he became a commissioner, has done excellent service. He is, besides, well fitted to preside over our local governing body by reason of hiB admirable qualities of head and heart, and is a gentleman fully deserving of the honour. It will easily be guessed that I mean Mr. Frank Wiswall, and I am sure that the ratepayers would be glad to hear that he had been placed in the chief office of honour in his native town.

There was no fanfare of trumpet at Widnes, or other sign of rejoicing over the arrival of the char- ter whico raises the town to the dignity of a muni- cipal borough. Perhaps the people are waiting until November before they demonstrate.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.
WITHDRAWAL OF MR. MOSS. THE SEARCH FOR A SUCCESSOR.

The announcement, on Tuesday, that Mr. Tom C. Edwards Moss, M.P. for the Widnes Division, in- tended not to contest the seat at the approaching election fell upon the electors like a bolt from the blue. The declaration was as sudden as it wat unexpected, and was received with the utmost surprise by Liberals as well as Conservatives. The news was first received at a meeting of the execu- tive of the Executive Council of the Widnes Divi- sion Conservative Association held at Liverpool on Monday. Mr. Moss in his communication assigned ill-health as the reason for his resignation, and he forwarded certificates from two doctors ordering him a prolonged change of air and pointing out the danger of the anxiety and worry of a contested election. The resignation was accepted with the utmost regret, and a deputation was appointed to wait upon several gentlemen with a view to one or other of them undertaking the contest in place of Mr. Moss. _

1 It will be remembered that not long ago Mr. Moss was somewhat seriously ill, and he went abroad with the object of restoring his weakened energies, and on his return it was made known that he had greatly benefitted by the change. Not many weeks ago he attended a crowded meeting in Widnes Drill Hall, end in the course of his speech expressed his determination to carry no the campaign with vigour, and urged his supporters to follow his example and leave no stone unturned to defeat Mr. Deacon, who was recognised as a most strong opponent. There is not the slightest doubt that the fight would have been a keen one ; the responsible officials on bath sides were prepared for a most arduous struggle, but the resignation of Mr. • Moss withdraws the strongest possible Tory candidate from Mr. Dea,con'ts path, and that gentleman'& prospects of success are thereby greatly enhanced. I On alb hands regret is expressed at the cause which has thrown upon tha Conservative party the necessity of searching for a candidate at the eleventh hour. Dur- ing the time he has represented the constituency, Mr. Moss has become personally very popular by his genia- lity and urbanity, and by the attention he gave to any requests or representations of his constituents, whatever colour their politics might be ; and it will be the unani- mous wish of all that lie may be speedily restored to complete health. At the first election after the re-distribution of seats- -1385, Mr. Moss polled 4,527 votes as against 2,650 polled by Mr. E. K. Muspratt, a majority in his favour of no fewer then 1,877 vo es. On that occasion Mr. Moss had the benefit of the Irish vote, which is a very large one. In the following year the result of the contest was— Moss (C), 3,719 ; A. Birrell (L), 2,92? ; majority, 792. It was stated on Thurs, lay,. apparently with authority, that Mr. George Pilkington..Major lValker (son of Sir , A4ll. Walker), Mr. H. H. Hornby, and Major Cross had been asked, and that eaeh had declined to fill the breach, and further that eight other gentlemen had also refused the proffered honour.. A CANDIDATE FOUND.

Saunders Gilliat, at present member for Clapham, was unanimously adopted the Conservative and Unioniat candidate for the Widnes division in the roam of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, who retires,

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was hell at the Town Ilall on Thursday night. Mr. James Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. A. Sallield and Mr. G. SI oss (clerk).

div.head: BOATMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN.
div.p: BOATMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN.

The minutes of the Committee showed that 80 parents had been summoned and 61 appeared, and 38 were pro- ceeded against before the magistrates. The visitors report stated that the average attendance at the schools had been 3,047, the highest figure which had yet been reached. file percentage of those on the rolls was 84.4, a number not exceeded more than once or twice. The report was considered highly satisfactory.—Dr. Gastaldi in moving the minutes, said although matters were more satisfactory than last year, yet there was a good deal to complain about with reference to the boat-people. The minutes were passed, and Dr. Gastaldi gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the Board petition Parliament to enact means for the proper educa- tion of local children.

div.head: WANT OF ACCOMMODATION.
div.p: WANT OF ACCOMMODATION.

The Committee appointed to consider the alleged want of school accommodation for infants in Newtown district had held a meeting at which the Clerk pre- -5e0t21 statistics showing the accommodation and aver- age attendance at all the schools in the town. Newtown Infants School was stated to be full, and the attendance officer produced a list of children who had applied and been unable to obtain. It was intimated that the managers were about to enlarge the school and the Committee considered that this would meet the exist- ing difficulty. The crowded state of Mill Brow Infants School was also mentioned. The Committee were of opinion that children living in that district might reasonably bo expected to attend Trinity Infants School where there was room for them thereby avoiding any necessity for exclusion at Mill Brow.—The minutes were approved.

_ _ SATINGS BANK FOR SCTIOOI., CHILDREK. On the 2tth May a meeting of the Board was held in Committee to receive the report of the Clerk with respect to the working of Savings Banks in elementary schools. After discussion it was recommended that a savings bank be established at each of the Board Schools, viz.. Green- way-road boys and girls and Mill Brow infants ; that the model rules issued by the post office be adopted. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Canon Wood seconded by Dr. Gastaldi.
AW APPLICATION.
Miss Annie Acton assistant mistress at Greenway-road, school made an application for an increase of salary: The matter was referred to the School Management Committee.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday:morning. Mr. 9.1. J. Grice presided,and there were present Messrs. Jas. Pritchard, H. White W. Timmins, E. W. Humphreys, P. Bisbrown, S. Taylor, W. R. Wass, W. Hankinson, F. Wiswall. F. A. Lake (clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker, (surVvyor), and Dr. McDougall (medical ofdcer). PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS.-IMPORTANT TOPPOPERTY OWNERS

The Highways and Buildings Committee, recom- mended that notices be served under section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1875, on the respective owners of the premises fronting, adjoining or abutting on the f Dllow- lug streets and passage to sewer, metal, channel, &c., such streets and passages, viz. : Leinster-st., Bentinck- st., Portland-st., Cawdor-st., Suffolk-st., Bracklev-st., Han key-st., Hope-st., Clarence-at-, Greek-st., Grove-st., Speakman-st., LlAndley-st., (part of—from Egerton-st., to Grove-st.,) Picow-st., Salisbury-st., Byron-st., Chau- cer-st., York-st., (as far as Hill-st.,) Hill-st., (from Victoria-road to York-st.,) Norfolk-st., Gresvenor-st., (to end of Hartley-st.,) Parker-st., (from Thomas-st., to Fisher-st.), Bold-st., (the whole length), Stanley-st., (as far as the buildings extend), Ann-st., (from Parker-st., toStanley-st.), Thomas-st., (the whole of),.Sewell-st•, (as far as the buildings extend), Spring-st., Penketh- lane, passage between Fox-st., and Salisbury-st., That the footways of the aforementioned streets be flagged or made with granolithic pavement or partly with one and partly - with the other at the dis- cretion of the Committee. In the event of any of such notices not being complied with and the Authority determining to execute the works mentioned or referred to therein, it is recommended that the expenses incurred be declared private improve- markt expenses, and that the consent of the Local Government Board be obtained to the spreading of the costs over a period of ten years.—That the expenses when incurred be repaid by the owners by quarterly instalments, except that when the expenses are under £lO they be repaid by annual instalments.—That in- terest at the rate of per cent, per annum be, charged over the rate at which the money is borrowed.—That resolution No. 1,329, which reads "That all streets before being adopted by the Board in future shall have the footways flagged and the streets otherwise made in accordance with the specifications of the Board," be amended by inserting the words "or made with grano- lithic pavement at the option of the Highways and Buildings Committee" after the word "flagged." Mr. Taylor moved and Mr. White seconded the adoption of the minutes, the formcr gentleman remarking that many of the property owners were workpeople and it would come very heavy upon them if they had to pay for the whole of this work in one year. The Board hoped to be able to borrow money at 3 percent., and the owners would be charged 4 per cent.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.p: Sr!IDAY CLOSING.

Mr. Humphreys asked the Chairman of the Parlia- mentary and Legal Committee whether it was proposed to taae any action with reference to the resolution passed two months ago referring the question of Sun- day Closing to that Committee. He was somewhat severely taken to task for suggesting that that course meant shelving the question, but inasmuch as nothing had teen done for two months he was not quite sure that his remarks were not justiiled.—Mr.. Pritchard said he had seen the secretary on two or three occasions with rerrard to calling the Committee together, but the Secret y had told him that it was too late as the Bill was r before Parliament, and that the.time had passed by wiien anything could be done in the matter. There was no attempt to shelve it ; he would call the members together if they thought it advisable.—The Chairman said he thought the Chairman of: the Committee had been a little remiss in not calling a meeting to consider the question and reporting to the Board at the next ineeting.—Mr. Pritchard: I shall have to put the respon- sibility ou the secretary. The Secretary :: So far as I am cormerned I will call a meeting. whenever I am in- structed. (Hear, hcar )—The discussion then ceased.

OPEN SPACES, Mr. Bisbrown said for several years past gentlemen who sat at that Board had given prominence in their election addresses to the establishment of open spaces or recreation grounds. lie was in full sympathy with a movement of that kind. But the want of ways and means ta carry the project into elect has been an insuperalde obstacle, and there did not seem to be any prospect of doing much in that directioo in the imme- diate future. Ile suggested that they would be supply- ing a want if in the suburbs of the town the Board would place a number of garden seats somewhat similar to those in the cemetery but much stronger. The Chairman said he quite sympathised with the object, and it was understbod that the Committee would deal with the subject. CYCLISTS A.ND.NORMALA ROAD. Mr. Lightburn drew attention to the inconvenience and danger to pedestrians in Norman-road caused through bicyclists using both sides of the road indis- , criminately, and he suggested that 8 or 10 feet on the near side of the road should he sat apart for pedestrians. ' the bieyelists to take the L. & N -W. railway side of the road.—Mr. Flumplareys suggested that the best solation would be to make a proper footpath.—The Law Clerk said the Board was not in any way liable and would not be juatified in spending any money on Norman-road. If the owners and occupiers in Norman-toad applied to the Board to make a footpath and expressed their will- ingness to contribute towards the cost then something might be done. They could not compel cyclists to keep to one side. but if they rode too fast or caused a nuis- ance then they became liable under the Public Act.—Mr. Lightuuril was of opinion that the matter had only to be mentioned and thecyclists would keep to one side.

Mr. William Barbour, of Bolton, who left England re- cently to start farming in Winnipeg, has been found dead in his farmhouse, shot through toe head. In the fire months ending on Tuesday the Glasgow shipbuilders have launched 150,000 tons of new shipping. This is very nearly the largest output on record, Fresh orders, however, are scarce.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND ZiEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND ZiEEN

AT WARRINGTON. In my humble estimation the answers of Mr Robert Pierpoint to the questions of the Amalgam-. ated Society of Railway Servants are worth reading. ! They should be placed under the heading—" A candidate in a corner,and how he gets out of it," or, rather, perhaps, " how he doesn't get out of it." Warrington is a working class constituency, and Mr. Robert Pierpoint feels that he should express a certain amount of sympathy with work- ing class aims and aspirations, even though he de- clines to have anything further to do with them. But his sympathy is of the inferior or one- sided kind.

Take, for instance, his reply to the question re- lating to the fixing of a maximum day of ten hours. lie is not in favour of this because it would be hard upon the man who has been out of work for a few weeks, and has run into debt, if he were not allowed to make up his lost time. What a truly sympathetic heart our Conservative candidate has for the industrious working-man who is eager to i put n more than ten hours work a day for the ,munificent overtime rates of pay which railway companies give !

But then, Mr. Pierpoint forgets to tell us why this industrious workman, who wants to do more than ten hours had been out of work at all,and had got into debt. Is it not a fact that large numbers of men are out of work simply because other men are practically compelled to work disgracefully long hours? Would not the very man he speaks about be helping to keep some other man out of a place by working more than the ten hours a day r Mr. Pierpoint's sympathy is of that peculiar order which flows out in copious streams towards the poor man who is pievented from working an ex- cessive number of hours, to the injury of himself' and his fellows,while there is not a particle of it to• spare for the man who can find no opportunity of earning a livelihood, owing to the overwork of others.

In Mr. Pierpoint's reply to the proposal that no man shall be allowed to drive an engine who is not provided with a certificate of competency from the Board of Trade, there is a neat piece of reasoning and a profound knowledge of the intricacies of rail- way management. "I would point out to you, says Mr. Pierpoint, " that, in IIOPI of the liability of heavy damages, setting aside other considerations, it is of the greatest importance to the railway com- panies that they should employ only the best men," Mr. Pierpoint might have " pointed out " while he was at it, that, "in view of the liability,' "it is of the greatest importance to the railway companies" that they should not keep men at work for an unreasonable numbar o hours. Yet what do we find ? That in accident after acci- oient it is discovered that some of the persons con- nected with them have been without rest for long stretches at a time. Mr. Pierpoint. I fancy, may rest assurred that railway servants know beist where their own shoe pinches, and that his weak display of Debating Society logic will not divert them from seeking a necessary reform.

I believe there are some iew Roman Catholics in Warrington, who vote on the Conservative side. They do so, notwithstanding the fact that it was the Liberals who gave them political emancipation, and a Tory Government, which in the destruction, by a colossal system of bribery, of the Irish Parlia- ment, when it was about to do justice politically to the Catholics of that country, delayed the measure for 20 years both for them, and their co-religionists in England. Conservative Roman Catholics in War rington have now another argument why they should vote Liberal in the coming election, and indeed I might say that it applies in the cases both of Nonconformists and Jews—who have experienced scant favour at Conservative hands— though we have not many of the latter in Warring- ton. A few weeks since Mr. John Ellis introduced into the House of Commons a bill to remove a hu- miliating and insulting disability under which Roman Catholics, Dissenters,and Jews are the prin- cipal sufferers, but which places them in invidious distinction with the Church of England, which is exempt from it. Mr. Ellis's Bill simply prc,posed to put all religious bodies on an equal footing with the State Church, so far as being able to acquire land compulsorily for church building sites. But the Tories unanimously objected to the principle of re- ligious equality laid down in the Bill,though in face of their impending appearance before the consti- tuency they did not dare to reject it directly, so disposed of it by the well-known dodge for doing away with obnoxious measures, that of referring it to committee. Keep this in mind Warrington Con- servative, Catholics, and Nonconformists.

I am sorry to say that, morally, Warrington has lately taken a decided turn for the worse. A few weeks since I commented on the fact that for nearly a year previous there had been a remarkable decrease of business at the police court in Warrington and adjacent places, and remarked that it seemed—so long had this happy state ot things continued—as though there was really a permanent improvement in the moral condition of Warrington and the whole dis- trict. The very first day, excepting Sunday, after my comments appeared there was, strange to say, a sudden and extraordinary increase of the business at the Warrington court, which brought it quite up to the standard of the bad old days. and this has steadily continued ever since. At Dareshury Ses- sions, this week, too, there has been a like reversion to the former objectionable state of things. One of our novelists says in a half serious way that when things are going well it is unlucky to say anything about it, and I declare I could not help thinking of his observation when I saw the sudden change for the worse that took place immediately after my remarks on the improve- ment. What has brought about the deplorable reversal of this it is most difficult to explain, for the increase has not been so muck in drunkenness . as in other offences, but there has certainly set in a . busy time for magistrates, their clerks, and the law- yers; and it seems as though there was a determina- tion on the part of the ill-disposed community to make my remarks look absurdly inapplicable, true though they were at the tine.

. Alderman liarrison, at the Warrington police court last week. proved himself to be profoundly erudite in the dialectics of inebriation by laying down a distinction between drunkenness and in- toxication. He cited the saying that a man is intoxicated when he knows what he is doing but does not care, and drunk when he neither knows nor cares what he is doing. It is the first time I have heard of any such subtle distinction— the only difference I supposed to exist V 741 a that intoxicated was the gentlemanly euphemism for diunk. Nuttall's Dictionary gives bluntly as the meaning of drunk—intoxicated. But if Alderman Harrison's definition were to be accepted our local constabulary would have to have their minds con— siderably exercised in deterrninating the exact shades of nice distinction between intoxication and> drunkenness with a view to widening their charges accordingly. This would be a truly mind-wreck- ing problem ; would qualify themr for their • superannuation allowance long before the present usual period.

-- Every constable would have th become a more. expert mind reader than Stuart Cumberland, or Irving Bishop to know whether an individual Was- drunk or intoxicated; and, if he could, there would remain the difficulty of satisfying magistrates and solicitors to accept their mind-reading as evidence. The policeman's lot, indeed, would not then be a happy one. There is a rough and ready defnition of drunkenness which it strikes me would be quite as good a working one as Alderman Harrison's, and ; would be a better guide for the constabulary. It is, as follows : • Not drunk is he who from the floor, Can rlso and loudly call for more ; But drunk is he who prostrate lies, Without the power to sseak or rise. M RUIN.

The wife of Captain Osborne gave birth to a daughter, on Tuesday morning. At the Edinburgh Police Court, on Monday, Andrew Riddell, a painter, was remanded on a charge of murder- ing Hugh Whiteford, a chimney sweep. Several accidental drowning cases are reported. At Bournemouth James A. Laney and Harold Fudge, young, men, were drowned while boating, and in Portsmouth Harbour a mann named Webb, of Hackney, lost his life. In the Tees, at Stockton, a shipwright named Flockton, and a boy named Bowes, were drowned. PROPERTY Skrx• On Tuesday, Messrs. J. B. and B. Leach, auctioneer, of St. Helens,oflered for sale at the Borough Sale Rooms, two freehold dwelling-houses, Nos. 55 and 51, Argyle-st., St. Helens, the gross rental being £24 per annum, the tenants paying rates. The bidding began at £3OQ, and the property was ultimately knocked down to Mr. Fox, Cowley Hill, St. Helens, for £it3s. The solicitors fpr the vendors were Messrs. fi. B, White and Bops, ot Warrington.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. Alfred Hargreaves. 14 William-St., who some time ago wee brought up at Warrington Police Court on a charge otattempting to commit suicide, but whose case was o,diourned to allow him to go on duty with the militia, was yesterday charged again, and, after some represen- tations by the police, was discharged. HE WANTED BRANDY. A young fellow, named James Taylor was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with having beeti drunk in Paradise-place, on the previous night. An officer found the prisoner apparently in a fit in Paradise-place, with a number of people around him. He WES taken to the Infirmary, but the doctor there *id he had only been " shamming," audit turned out this was one of the young man'a dodges for getting brandy. As he was being brought from the Infirmary to the Felice Station lie used some very violent language; being apparently much enraged that his little scheme Should have miscarried. He was tined 53. and costs. NEEFT FROM TIIE FATTEN ARMS. Charles Heaton, of 7 Wakefield-st., Warrington, was citarged on remand at the borough Police court, on Wed- nesday, with stealing frem the Pattea Arms Hotel, on Saturdav night, two pairs of trousers, one vest, and a leather belt, value 155., the property of Frederick Gilbert Of the Huts, Big Field. near Runcorn. The prisoner leaded guilty. They were drinking in the hotel together and somehow or other the gas went out for a few minu- tee, and when it was lit both the prisoner and the I articlea were missing. The matter was reported to the' police, and about six o'clock on Sunday morning-the prisoner was apprehended at his lodgings, with a bundle oktttaining the missing things in his possession. He said behad bought them. The owner of them was discovered after tbe prisoner's remand.—Heaton said he had been drinking tor the last fortnight, and did not know how be came into possession of the articles.—He was com- mitted to prison for 14 days' hard labour. THEFT OF CIGARETTES BY BOYS. Prederlek George Wale, son of Patrick Wade, 15, Gee- -1%, and Patrick Lennardy, son v 4 Ilricl,;ot Warburton-st., boys, were charged at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, with stealing at about half-past nine on Saturday night, a box of cigar- ettes, the property of Thomas Morris, provision dealer, h. Foundry-St. Mr. Morris sent his little boy to buy Om box of cigarettes, and as he was coming hack the /prisoners met him and Wade snatched the box from him, and ran away, followed by the other prisoner. Inspector Spinks about half-past two on Sunday morn- -tog saw the prisoner and another boy pear St. Paul's church, and they tried to get away, but with the assist- asnee of a lamplighter he took them into custody. Packets of cigarettes were found on each of them, also on three Other boys who had been in their company, and all five Were in Court. The prisoners ma re ordered to be de- tained till 6 p.m., and to he hKI with six strokes Of the birch rod each. The other three lads who were standing near the dock,thoug,h not in it, were cautioned. CHARGE OF ASSAULTING A WOMAN. Daniel Couglitn,a navvv,wa's charged before the War- rington magistrates on Monday with :wanking Mary Connor, married woman, on Saturday night in Hill- st.—The evidence of Mary Connor. and Annie Grant was as follows :—The complainant and the prisoner both lodged in the common lodging house in Hill-st., and the prisoner was eating his supper when a man named James Butler who lodged there, came in. The prisoner had a quarrel with him, and as he was in dan- ger of being stabbed with the knife with which the pri- boner had been eating, the complainant rushed in , between them and seized the bltde with her hand, and the prisoner drew it away, cutting it so, that she had to have the wound dressed at the IMlrmary. The wound was quite aecidental. —Detective-Sergeant Monaghan gait! Mrs. Connors statement to him was very much stronger than that she had made in court. He believed also was afraid to speak. She told him that when she came back from the Infirmary Coughlin made a second • attack upon her. The case was disnihe ed. PASSING AN OBSOLETE INDIAN COIN. At the Warrington Magistrates' Court, on Monday, Patrick Linskey. labourer, 6, Lilford-5t., and John Whittaker. hawker and greengrocer, of Friar's Green, Were charged with stealing on Sunday night two bottles Of herb beer, value id, and is. 11d., the property of Mary Ann Sutton, a widow, aged about 70 years, of 19, Pennell-st.—Linskey pleaded guilty and Whittaker not guilty.—The Chief Constable said about nine o'clock on nunday night prisoners went to the Grove beerhouse, And asked for a glass of beer each,and on being supplied, tendered as payment to Mrs. Roberts, a silver coin, which she saw was an Indian rupee. She handed it back, and withdrew the beer, warning them that they would get into trouble if they did not mind. They, however, niade the same attempt at the Rose Inn beerhouse, and MreJackson,before supplying them with the beer-showed the coin to her husband, who said it was an Indian rupee, and that it was no payment, and returned it. The prisoners afterwards passed the coin on Mrs. Sutton, obtaining two glasses of herb beer and is. 11d, change for the coin—Alderman Harrison : She thought it was a florin P—The deputy magistrates' clerk :It IS the size of a florin.—Evidence was given proving the passing of the coin, the subsequent discovery of the fraud, and the men's arrest.—Alderman Harrison, on the coin being shown to the Bench, remarked that it appeared to he a lona fide coin of the realm, and many money changers would change it fonts value —The Chief,Constable : That does not do away with the felonious intent.—Linskey was sentenced to seven days', and Whittaker the tenderer of the coin ton month's hard labour.—The coin, it may be mentioned, was an old East Indian Company's rupee,now obsolete. HOUGH ON A SOLDIEB.—A POLICE CONSTABLE SPOKEN To. - .

Thomas Walsh, a young soldier, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, with having I been drunk in Buttermarker-st., the previous night; and with having assaulted P.C. Newey. Walsh appeared to have been very much bruised about the face, one of his eyes being comple.tely swollen over, and his head bandaged, owing to a severe cut at the back of it. P.p. Newey said that at about half-past 11 at night he saw rho prisoner and another soldier with a prostitute, and making a good deal of noise. He told them to move en, and, after a short altercNtion, Walsh knocked his helmet off with a cane, and strlick him two or three blows on the head. Re closed with Walsh and threw him down, the cut in the head being caused by a fall on the kerb- stone, and the bruises on his face being also caused by falling on the ground. Other officers gave evidence as to Walsh being drunk, " Police constable Corcoran mentioning that he had previously told him to move away. Inspector Spinks said that Walsh's head bled so much that they took him to the In- nrmary to have it dressed. The prisoner said that the officer, with very little provocation, got hold of him by the collar, and butted him in the face with his head, and, altogether used him very roughly. The other sol- dier said P.C. Newey kicked the prisoner on the legs. 'he Chairman said it was evident that Walsh had had much the worse of the encounter, and he would be dis- missed. The Bench afterwards spoke to P.C. Newey, and advised him always to act courteously to others, and never to use more violence than was absolutely necessary. The Chief Constable said he had always been tamg,,ht that a prisoner should be brought to the Police Station without a rent or a scratch if possible, and in this case he should require a written statement from P.C. Newey.

ARTFUL FEMALES.—D.S. MONAGHAN SMARTLY UNRAVELS THE PLOT. Mary Garrity, who is a widow, living in Smith-St., and Mary Docherty, the wife of a labourer who resides in the neighbourhood of Dial-st., were charged at the War- rington Borough Court, on Tuesday, with stealing £2185., the property of an old man, named John Reynolds. rue facts of the case came out pretty much as follows. The old man Reynolds, who is seventy years of age, but, Judging from his palsied hands, hardness of hearing, and general appearance of decay, might be considered several years older, was walking through the streets with money in his pockets when he met widow Garrity, whose husbarsd he used to know. After some con- versation, Mrs. Garrity invited Reynolds to her house, a "deplorable little hut in a back-yard" according to the words of the Chief Constable. When he got there he found Mrs. Docherty also in possession. They had some drink together, and eventually Mrs. Garrity invited Reynolds upstairs. He assented, but he had no sooner got to the top of the stairs than she put her hand in his pocket and picked out the money, which was tied together in a piece of cloth, and she and Mrs. Docherty bolted out of the house with the I spoil. Some time after information was given to the police, and D.S. Monaghan was put in charge of the case. When he went to Mrs. Garritty she denied hav- ing any money, but when she had taken her shoes and I stockings off in obedience to a request, a sovereign and i half a sovereign dropped out of one of the stockings.— I, D.S. Monaghan next went to 'Mrs. Docherty's house, and she, too, denied having any money, but, on being told she would have to go to the police office, she at- tempted to push past Monaghan and he noticed that she dropped a half-sovereign and put her foot on it, and seeing one of her hands closed, he asked her te open it and there found another half-sovereign. The I Chairman, in giving the verdict of the Bench, said it I was an abominable case and Reynolds certainly would not have deserved much' sympathy if he had lost his I money. Garritty was sent for two months' hard labour and Docherty for one month. A DRUNKEN FREAK. OF A RUNCORN PURLICAN AND OTHERS. At the Daresbnry Petty Sessions on Tuesday, John ' Massey. landlosci of the Albion Vaults beerhouse, Nelson street, Runcorn, Daniel Massey, coal dealer, residing next door to him, John Brown, of the same street and James Clayton, of Ellesmere-street. Runcorn, were charged with stealing between 5.30 p.m. and 6.30 p.m., a wooden box and a dress, a vest and a club scarf, left in the box, the property of Thomas Nor- man, from the house of John Robinson at Preston Brook on the 26th of May. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, of Runcorn I appeared for the defence.—Wm. Lowe deposed to the defendants coming home in a shandry not sober, but not" that drunk" and John Massey, his employer, tell- ing him to put a box which Brown had, into the hayloft, and cover it with hay. It was put into the loft, and Brown and Clayton hid it under the hay. —Thomas Norman said he left the box in the care of John Robinson at Preston 8r00k,12 months ago.—Emily Larton deposed that that day week she saw the articles in the box in the house at Runcorn, where Robinson had previously lived. She locked the door, and brought the key away on the Wednesday night. On Saturday morn- ing the lock and chain of the door had gone.—John Robinson, painter,said he left the box there on the Tues- day, and on Thursday evening he found the back door forced open, and his little boy went into the house, and came back and said the box was gone.—John Taylor, farmer, of Asliton,said he saw the defendant on the 26th inst., with a cart in front of the door in which was a box.—P.C. Fryer said on the same evening he was going to take the prisoners' names for trespassing in pursuit of game, and he saw the box in the cart, and in the box he found the dress produced. He afterwards apprehended them for the robbery. They all denied the theft of the articles. He found the box in John Massey's loft, under about 12 trusses of hay, and also the vest amongst the hay.—Thos. Booth, greengrocer, Church-st., Runcorn, Wm. Philips, and John Peers, testified to the previous good character of the defendants.—Mr. Hum- phreys said he would not deny that the box was taken by the defendants or some of them, but there was not that aninzus furandi which was of the essence of larceny. They were practically all drunk at the time, and they ' thought it would be a sort of freak to run off with the box. Lowe was mistaken when he said John Massey asked him to bring in the box. The two Masseys owned the houses they lived in and were not likely to run the risk of criminal proceedings for the sake of stealing things of such small value. The fact that the lock and chain disappeared from the back door while they were in custody proved that other persons than themselves had been about the premises.—The defendants were fined £1 each and costs.

yard in Locfge-lane on Tuesday last, ing violently assaulted his wife on the 21st May.—Thomas Haynes, son of the prisoner, said his father gave him the petticoat and told him to go into Tunstall's pawn- shop with it. He went, and they gave him 9d. for the article.—Detective Monaghan deposed that he charged the prisoner with the theft, and he replied " What they say is all lies." The magistrates dismissed this charge on account of the son's evidence being unsatisfactory.— The second charge, that of assaulting his wife, was then I preceeded with.—Mary Jane Haynes said that on the 20th May the defendant assaulted her in a most violent manner. He gave her a black eye, and kicked her with his clog. Evidence in support of this was given by al neighbour, and the defendant was committed to prison for a month with hard labour. Tnerr OF A SOVEREIGN.—George Wade, lately of Liverpool, was charged with stealing on the previous afternoon, at the Bear's Paw Inn, 13uttermarket-st., a sovereign, the property of Samuel; Silcock, the landlord i of that nn. The prisoner was in the inn, and asked for a new pipe, and the landlady soon after placed the sovereign on the inside counter, and was absent from the bar for half a minute, and missed the sovereign on her return, but a dirty pips had been placed on the counter. She informed her husband, and the prisoner told him that the pipe was his, he not having been supplied with a clean one. The landlord asked him to turn out his money, but he said he could not as he had none. He was given into custody, and at the police station a sovereign was found upon him, and on being charged with stealing it at the inn he replied, "Oh, that's all right."—The prisoner pleaded guilty, but said" Thad been a bit fresh or I would not have done it."—He was committed to prison for a month's hard labour. WEDNESDAY.— Before Captain Wallington (chairmen), Major Pickmere, and Mr. John White. CHARGE OF THEFT—John and Thos. Kelly, brothers, were charged with stealing at buttonwood on the night of the 29th of May, 15s. 51., the property of Martin Cooney. Mr. Percy Davies defended the prisoners.— The complainant said that on Sunday night he had been at the Chapel beerhouse, in company with a man named McDonald, and opposite the Elm Tree beerhouse he saw six or seven men, including the prisoners, standing. At that time he remembered having a call to make, and McDonald left him. On his coming back the men were still there, and some of them seized him and commenced carrying him face downwards when the money fell out of Ins pocket, and the prisoners picked it up, and went away with it, and the other men left him. The night was very dark. He screamed when the men were carrying him. He had been in the Chapel Inn from 8 to 10 o'clock.—Evidence was called for the defence from which it appeared that a woman standing near saw a scuffle but heard no screaming, and she thought they were all merely larking together. On the ' prisoners being apprehended John replied that he had seen nothing of the money, and Thomas that Cooney had followed him down the road and asked him for it, bus he told him he had not got it, which was true. He came up to them and complained of having been robbed, and they recommended him to go to the police station. He went part of ;the way to it, then returned, and told them they would hear more about the matter.—The Bench dismissed the case. NON-MAINTENANCH 017 • WlFlL—Matthew Littler, collier, of Haydock, was charged with non-compliance with a separation order made April 4th, 1883, by not contributing to the maintenance of his wife, Harriet. The case had been adjourned from the previous court to allow the defendant an opportunity to prove the troth of allegations of immorality made by him against his wife. The amount claimed was £8 15s. Evidence was called in support of his statements, but failed to estab- lish his charges. and the Bench made an order for pay- ment of the amount, in default two months' imprison- ment.—The defendant, who had only paid his wife 30s. under the order, said he could not pay the amount claimed, and would not, and lie was sent to jail.

AN UNLICENSED DOG.--Elenry Robinson, Dutton, for keeping a dog without a license was fined ss. IN PURSUIT OP GAME.—George Sefton, labourer, of Warrington, was charged that on the 14th of May at Grappenhall he was found in possession of two rabbits, also that he was found in possession of a net and pegs used for taking game, having been unlawfully in pur- suit of game. Wm. Rustage, of Warrington, was charged with aiding and abetting Sefton.. P.C. Milling- ton proved the case.—Wm. Oakes and Wm. Eastham gave evidence to prove an alibi for Restage, and he was dismissed, Saf ton being fined 10s. and Costs. BREACHES OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ANIMALS ACT. —Peter Collins,George Holt, Martha Faulkener, Edmund Taylor, William Taylor, and Jas. Warburton, farmers, were charged with causing cattle to be removed from Carrington and Partington to Appleton, on the 27th of April, and William Collins and John Collins, labourers, were charged with moving the same.—lt appeared that the farmer defendants had been misled through being informed that the regulations were rescinded, and a Carrington constable telling them he Neould let them know if a licence was required, but not doings°, though he saw them removing the cattle.—The Bench were informed that the regulations had been withdrawn a fortnight.—They considered that the defendants had rea- son to suppose the restrictions were " off," and dismissed the cases. DRUNK.—William Mueller, drunk on the 25th of April at Little Leigh, was dismissed on payment of costs. CATTLE STRAYING.—GeOr."O Hewitt,for allowing cattle to stray at Little Leigh, on the 18th of May, had to pay

COSI& RIDING Wrrnour Retws.—Alfred Bell, for driving without reins, at Little Leigh, on the 11th of May, had to pay 34. Bd. costs ; Luke Feeney, for a like offence at Appleton, on the 18th of May, had to pay costs. Doe AT Litres—Edwin Ellison, for allowing dog to be at large at Appleton, on the 24th of May, was fined 4s. ed. costs. CHARGE AGAINST A LITTLE LEIGH PUBLICAN.—Mary Ann Cowap, landlady of the Horns Inn, Little Leigh was charged with keeping open her house for the waled, also with selling intoxicating liquor, during prohibited' hours, on the 22nd of May, and with allowing beer to be consumed on the premises on the same occasion and Alfred Halsey, and John Dockerty,aged,l6,were charged with being then found on the premises. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, of Runcorn, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, for the defence.— Mr. Humphreys stated that on the morning of Sunday, May 22nd, Police-Sergeant Dutton and P.C. Richardson went into a farm building about 50 yards from the inn and watched it. They reached there about 20 minutes past three, and about 10 minutes after Bali, a stranger enter the house, by the back door, which was left open till about five o'clock. Then it was closed by a man apparently in Mrs. Cowap's employ. A few minutes before this, another man came to the front door and knocked. A head came out of the win- dow, and shortly afterwards Mrs. Cowap came down and let a man in bythe back door. He remained about ten minutes, and they went away towards Bartington. About five minutes to eight two other men came to the back door, and were admitted by defendant's son and remained in the house • an hoUr, then went in the direc- tion from which they came. About a quarter, to nine Halsey, a railway porter, working at Acton Bridge Station, entered the house by the back door, and about, 20 minutes to 10 Towel, and another man named John Dockerty were supplied by Mrs. Cowap at the back door with a pint of beer each, for which they paid. The police left the building in which tkey were concealed, , and went near the inn and saw the beer served and paid for.—Police-Sergeant Dutton corroborated this state- ment, and in reply to Mr. Brown said the barn he was concealed in belonged to the opposition publican, but they were not there at his suggestion or with his know- ledge.—The defence was that Towey met Lockerty who , worked pear the inn, and was newly from Ireland anc they having been acquainted there, Towey took him to' the inn to treat him telling him he must say like him he came from Northwich, and they both told the landlady this. Halsey was on Sunday duty and came frcm Hart- ford,and had breakfast at half-past live,and walked some distance to get the signal lamps in and do other hard work. Ile went to the inn for some beer and bread and cheese. The other callers were men who came out that way to fish, and had slept, as was the custom with such men, in the open air all night.—The magistrates, after about ten minutes' private consultation, convicted Mrs.. Cowap on the second charge,and fined her 404. and costs for the offence. Halsey was fined ss. and costs and Dockerty discharged with a caution.—Mr. Browne said Mrs. Cowap had been 23 years in the house without a previous conviction, and would now have to leave it if this conviction were sustained; but gave notice of ap- peal against it.-1 he Chairman: That cannot make any difference in our decision. GAME TRESPASS.---ThOMES Davies, Ship Canal navvy, for being found tprpassing in search of game at Keke- wick on Sunday night, was fined ss. and costs. Summer-like weather prevailed, whilst the chits mustered their full strength. Sale won the toss, and on batting first Messrs. N. C. Browning and Ireland faced Messrs. Smith and J. J. Crosfield. A DRUNKEN AND HEARTLESS MOTHER.

At the Warrington Police Court,yestcrday, before Alderman Harrison (chairman) and Alderman Wright, Catherine Benson, of 37, Scotland-road,was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., soon after midnight, on the 31st ult., and also with exposing her child, about three weeka old. Mr. Ruckton appeared for the prosecutionwon the second charge, on behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children.—P.O. 17 said he found the woman drunk,sitting on a doorstep, and using very bad language. She bad a child in her lap,more like a bundle of rags than anything else. She had two bottles of beer. She was not fit to have a child in her care. Sergeant Cheney carried the child to the Police Station, and made it a bed of rugs. It seemed to have no life in it, and was a long time in coming round. It was blue with the cold, through exposure, without clothes. Witness took the woman to the station.— Inspector Spinks said but for the police the child would not have been alive now. The defendant told him she was confined in Prescot Union. and she did not know where he was.—Mrs. Daley, wife of a lodging-house keeper, Scotland-road, said the woman came to her house on the night of May 31st, about is quarter:to 11, drunk. She had a bottle ef beer with her, and the child, which was wrapped up in an old shawl. She did not ask for lodgings.—Mrs. Monaghan gave corroborative evidence, and said the child was cold and emaciated, and she thought it was going to die.—Mrs. Kilkehny said the woman was trying to pour beer out ofia bottle down the child's throat, and because it would not drink it said with an oath that she would choke it. Witness then brought a constable to hen—The Chairman said the case was one of the most revolting cases he ever heard of. He never heard of more inhuman treatment to a poor little baby. She was a disgrace to her set. She would have to go to prison for two months with hard labour. The poor unfortunate little child would have to go with, her, but it would be looked after by the prison authorities.—Mr. Ruckton said the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children would look alter the child when the mother cams out of prison.

Much excitement continues to prevail at Coventry ever the vicar's rate prosecutions. Seventy-eight sum- monses were down for hearing at the Police Court on Wednesday, and a great crowd, after parading the streets, assembled in the vicinity Of the building. The magistrates were, however, informed that the Bishop of Worcester was coming to Coventry with a view to settl- ing the dispute, and on this the magistrates adjourned the hearing of the summonses for a fortnight.

As the result of further private communieations which have passed between the Parliamentary leaders, 1 the First Lord of the Treasury is not now likely to be pressed by the Front Opposition Bench to, make before Whitsuntide his promised statement as to the intentions of the Government with regard to public business but it will be made soon after the re-assembling of Parlia- ment. Meantime it is still understood on all hands, al- ' though not officially announced, that the dissolution is to take place in or about the last week in June, and it is in order to hasten the progress of Supply with this ' view that the Whitsuntide vacation is to be restricted this year to rather less than a week, instead of extend- ing over the whole of next week. As the coming , dissolution will oecurr at nearly the same time of the year as that of 1886, something may be learned from the sequence of events in that year. On 10th of June, 1886, Mr. Gladstone announced that the dissolution would take place on the 26th. All conten- tious Bills were droppedond the financial business was woutid up in six days. The Appropriation Bill was brought in on the 16th, the Indian Budg9t on the 21s8. Parliament was prorogued on the 25th June, and the dissolution took place on the following day. The parallel of the present Parliamentary crisis with that of 1886 is further carried out by the incidence of the , Whitsuntide Recess. In 1886 the House of Commons adjourned after a morning sitting on the Friday before Whit Sunday, resuming on the following Thursday an arrangement precisely followed out in the present session. Mr. W. Redmond, M.P., speaking at the National League meeting at Dublin on Tuesday, said as far as be knew, the Parnellites were about to fight every constitu- ency from the Giant's Causeway to Cape Clear.

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION. LETTER TO THE LONDON TRADES COUNCIL. • As announced by Mr. Gladstone at the Memorial Hall, on Tuesday night, the right hon, gentleman had written to Mr: George Shipton, Secretary to the Lon- , don Trades Council,expressing his willingness to receive a deputation on the Eight Hours Question. In continu- ance of the previous correspondence Mr. Shipton had forwarded on behalf of the London Trades Council copies of the resolutions passed on the subjeat by Trades Union Congresses and the May Day Hyde Park Demon- stration, with other explanatory information presenting , the case of the working people on the question. The following is the last letter received by Mr. Shipton :- 1, Carlton-gardens, „ May 31st, 1892. - Dear Sir,—l have to thank you for your letter of the 27th, to which I should have replied earlier had I not happened' to leave town on the 28th before its arrival. The resolutions when brought together, and when com- bined with the explanations you are good enough to give me, supply me I think with a sufficiently definite view of the desires expressed by the Trades Council to enable me, if the Council desires a personal conference, to enter into it with advantage. In that event I should be happy to see any gentleman whom the Council may depute for the purpose at this house on Thursday, June 16, at 2 p.m. I name this eomparatively distant date as the Whitsuntide recess is immediately approaching. I do not know of how many members it may be desired to compose the deputation, but the state of my hearing leads mete mention that the more conversaiionat our conference may. be the more thoroughly I shall profit by it.—l remain, dear Sir, your very faithful, W. E. GLADSTONE,
Mr. G. Shipton. Mr. Shipton has summoned a special meeting of the Axecutive of the London Trades Council to consider this letter, and to decide what action shall be taken thereon.

div.head: LATE MR. E. GREENALL.
div.p: THE LATE MR. E. GREENALL.

, At the Daresbury Petty Setsions on Tuesday, Mr. J. C. Pair, who was presiding, saidhe felt lie could nap commence -the,,busipees of the court without recording the very deep sense felt by the Bench Of the loss they had sustained in the. death of their Chairman and paying their sincere tribute to the memory Of i very good, and efficient man, lie need not remind them that until a very short. time ago he attended the court most assiduously, and devoted himself fully to his public duties. ,It was always his endeavour in that court to administer justiee without fear or favour and without respect to persons, and at the same time his genial and temperament always in- duced him to see mitigating circumstances' irit were possible, and to temper justice with mercy. He felt that they all wished to place on record their sincere sympathy and condolence with his widow and family in their irreparable loss.—Mr. Jenkins said on behalf of those who had been accustomed to practise in that court, he re-echoed the sentiments which the Chairman had so well expressed. Nothing that could fall from his lips could possibly add to the kindly expression of the feeling which the Bench and all of them cherished for him who had gone.

div.head: PA.ItIt'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.
div.p: PA.ItIt'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.

ANOTHER AMALGAMATION. The directors of Parr's Banking Company Limited announce that they have arranged with the direc- tors of the Alliance Bank Limited, for the Amalga- mation of the business of that bank with Parr's Banking Company, Limited, as from 31st December 1891, on terms which they are satisfied will be mutually advantageous to the shareholders of both companies. The arrangement will involve the allocarion to the shareholders of the Alliance Bank of 16,000 shares of £lOO in Parr's Banking Company Limited, .£2O paid, in lieu of their present capital of £BOO,OOO paid up, and in return the whole assets of the Alliance Bank will be transferred to Pares Bank- ing Company. less ..£160,000, which is to be retained for distribution amongst their shareholders, Parr's Banking Company assuming at the same time the liabilities of the Alliance Bank. As a bonus to the shareholders in Parr's Banking Company, 1,500 new shares, together with 500 shares at present at the disposal of the directors, will be distributed amongst the existing shareholders, in the proportion of one share to each 16 now held, and at the price of £5O per share, being £2O for capital and £3O for premium, thus afford- ing a bonus on each share allotted of £2B taking the present market value of the share at £7B. The capital of the company will thus be raised to £5,000,000, of which £1,000,000 will be paid up, and the reserve fund, now £390,000 in the case of Parr's Banking Company, and £280,000 in the case of the Alliance Band—together £67o,ooo—will be raised to £1,000,000. Six of the direc- tors of the Alliance Bank are to join the board of Parr's Banking Company. 'The name of the company is to be changed to" Parr's Banking Compady and the Alliance Bank ,LI nited." The premises of the Alliance Bank, Limited, in Bartholomew-lane, 8.C., are admirably situated, and will afford ample accommodation for all the purposes of the arr,a gamated bank. A meeting of the shareholders of Parr's Banking Com- pany, Limited, is to be called at an early date to con- sider, and, if approved, to pass the special resolutions requisite to carry the above arrangements into effect. The directors also state that " Since the directors last addressed the shareholders, they have had to deplore ' the decease of two of their most prominent and esteemed colleagues, Mr. N. Eckersley and Mr. Edward Greenall, who bad rendered mast valuable seruices to the Bank, Mr. Eckarsley having been a director and an active , member cf the Select Committee since 1873, and deputo- 1 chairman of the Board since 1883, and Mr. Greenall having been chairman of the Select Committee for nearly 25 years. The directors elected Mr. Alfred Turner to be deputy-chairman and Mr. Eckersley's son, Mr. N. ffarington Eckersley, to a seat at the Board, and the shareholders will be asked to confirm the latter appointment at their next meeting. Mr. Charlton Parr, having resigned the chairmanship of the Select Committee after the last general meeting, xpressed at the same time his wish to be relieved of the duties of the chairmanship of the Board, but in con- equence of the illness of the late Mr. Eckersley, then I 4puty,,;,„;ona ft, he kindlyHecornesecennttel, wye dytohwoledtrhe , 1.0 efilie fce- for some montlui rated his desire to retire frilrn tht coarMkroship, as he was unable to give the fatitaliPCl taention to the busi- ness of the bank rendered necessary by its extension. 'The directors relttetabtlY agreed to accept his resigna- tion of the office Which he had held with such signal advantage to the bank since 1874. He remains a direc- tor and a Member of the Select Cemmittee. Mr. Alfred Turner, who had been a director and an active member of the Select Committee since 1883, has been appointed to succeed Mr. Parr as chairman of the Board."

div.head: STRANGE CHARGE OF CRUELLY TO
div.p: A STRANGE CHARGE OF CRUELLY TO

A CHILD. E2STRAORDIIAItY CONFLICT OF MEDICAL EVIDENCE. At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Thesday, be- fore Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), the Hon. G. Tal- bot, and Messrs. J. Marton, C. Markin, W. Long,and W. C. Jones, Henry White, of Cross-lane, Latchford. employed' on the Ship Canal, was charged wtli cruelly ill-treating, on May 12th, Blanche Whtte.bip daughter, aged 14, by severely beating her with a rope. Mr.Longton, of Wartington,apPettred for the prosecution, on behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children,and Mr, Forshaw, of Warrington, for the defence.—The child stated that on the Saturday in question a shilling was put on a box in her father's house, and her brother took it. Her mother charged her with stealing it, and partially undressed her and thrashed her about the shoulders. Mrs. White then sent for witness's father, and be compelled her to completely strip, and beat her tibout the hack and other parts of her body alth a rope not the thick- ness of ker little finger. He did not hurt her very much or make her bleed, be told him she had taken the shilling to avoid being beaten. She went to a policeman and showed hittilgid his wife, how she bad been beaten. Her father sent leer to a relative's at Lydney to get her away from bEt bad companions. She was there not quite a day, etien west to her grandmother's in Cauces- tershire.—st Mr. Forshaw : Witness ha,d taken loaves from her tithet's house, sold them, and spent the money. She told her father she had left the shilling at Barber's, and he went there, and on coming back, gave her the thrnshing. She deserved it.—P.C. Millington said On Thursday evening the gill came to his house crying, and was quite nervous and upset, and complained of her father having thrashed her. His wife and he examined her. There were stains of blood on her underclothing, and on raising it it stuck to her like a plaster. From the neck all down the back she was nothing but wounds and weals. She had scores of wounds. He reported the matter to the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children.—By Mr...For:thaw : The defendant bore a very good character. Witness should say lie thrashed her very severely. Me had never seen a child in such a state in•his life. The defendant's wife had been to complain to him. She was a little deranged in her mind.—Miriam Martha Jones, married woman, the child's grandmother, of Bream, near Lydney, said on the 14th of May. the , child came to her, and made a complaint to her. She had a bruise on her forehead and a black eye. She had 17 wounds on her, and her underclothing had blood on it. She was taken suddenly away from her house without her consent by someone sent for her. Witness had no ill feeling against the defendant.—Mr. Forshaw : She herself does not say she had a black eye.—Witness : because she is afraid.—ty Mr. Longton ; Members of her family are in the habit of visiting me.—Dr. Joseph, deposed that he examined the child on May 28th and found her suffering from severe contusions on the left side of the back. They could not have been produced if she had been thrashed with her clothes on, unless some very thin elothing.—Mr.For- shaw said his client did not deny thrashing the girl, but he positively denied having inflicted upon her anything but a reasonable and proper chastisement, that was, only five or six strokes on her back with a birch rod.— Temperance Emily Philips, married woman, of Birken- head, said the defendant was her brother. The com- plainant's father brought her to witness's home about eight days after the 12th of May, and said she had been stealing money, and he wanted to get her away I her bad companions. The Inspector came to her house and wanted to examine the child. She had so bruises on her forehead, and no black eye and no blood on her underclothing which she said was the same she wore after being thrished. She was quite lively, and witness did not consider it necessary to examine lien—Alf:led Robins, ship canal foreman, gave the defendant an excellent character.—Dr. Ronald, of Latchford, said he examined the child on the 29th of May,and saw nothing except two faint lines on the left side of the back. She told him she had the same clothes on as she put on after -being thrashed ; and he found no bloodstains on them. She said her father gave her five or six strokes; and her mother two over the shoulders. The mother was a little weakminded and might isle complaints unnecessarily. He had Yen marks prominent four weeks after a severe thrashing.— Dr. Cannel!, of Warrington, said he examined the child the previous afternoon, but found no marks except two on the left side of the hack probably caused by her stays. There were no marks of blood on her underclothing, which she said was the same she wore at the time in question. He considered the case the most trumped up one he ever heard of. He thought the • Bench should examine the girl in the ante-room. He did not believe Dr. ioseph found any contusions.—The Bench retired. and ih a few minutes had the girl brought into the ante- room, and on returning some minutes later, they dis- missed the case.
