div.head: Eettero to the Obttor.
div.p: Eettero to the Obttor.
WARRINGT9N RATES.

Sir,—! am not at all surprised to see Mr. Beswick's letter in last Saturday's issue. lam only surprised there are not more complaints. My improvement rate has just taken a leap forward of 4s. Next thing we shall have some member of the Town Council standing up and proposing the increase of salary of another batch of Corporation officials and clerks.—Yours, &c., A STRUGGLING RATEPAYER.
THE WARRINGTON CANDIDATES AND QUES-

TIONS BL RAILWAY MEN. • Sir,—The trail of red herring is so apparent in Mr. Dakin's letter, it becomes an easy matter to arrive at a safe conclusion with regard to it. He either belongs to the corn mon order of Tory bigots, and desires to be- little and minimise the praiseworthy action of a section of his fellow workmen, or else he wrote that letter in order to curry favour with the officials of the London and North Western. What other motive could he possibly have in thus publicly classing himself in Carlyle's famous majority? He need not have gone to so much trouble surely, to tell us what every Trade Unionist knew before. It is true the figures he quotes speak for themselves, but only to emphasize the lamentable fact that there are a vast deal more non-society men than Society men. But it is also true that history and experience prove over and over and again that 90 good men and true, banded together in a common cause, would obtain more concessions to labour in 12 months, than 400 outsiders would in a lifetime. It is too late in the day to ques- tion the good already down by Societies, and I fully believe that even the outsiders when the time for action arrives, will to a large extent be found in full sympathy with the action taken by the Warrington Branch, con- sequently, it is reasonable to expect that their votes will be influenced very much by the answers given to the questions submitted in their interests to each can,- didate.—Yours truly,

div.head: WM. KNOWLES, Trinity Place, Warrington, June 2nd, 1892.
div.p: WM. KNOWLES, Trinity Place, Warrington, June 2nd, 1892.

Sir,—Allow me, as Secretary of the local branch of the Amalgated Railway Servants, a few words in reply to the misguided, and misapplied views, contained In Joseph Dakin's letter of last week. I feel sure it would be useless to argue the point with him, but still I am, by duty, bound to show both him and others that there is a very wide difference between the actual facts of the case, and the inference he wishes to draw. In the first place, our Society does not and never did profess to represent the thoughts and views of all railway servants. What it does represent is, the interests and well being of the general body of employees, outsiders as well as members. Can Joseph Dakin see the difference? Our Society, in order to be practical, has drawn up a series of questions, directly affecting the railway-workers interests, and, naturally enough, we in Warrington, have submitted those questions to our local Parliament- ary Candidates. Having now obtained complete answers, although the issue is left perfectly open to every one, yet we, individually, are better able to judge for our- selves which candidate best represents our interests, and therefore,if we are worth our salt as practical and sensible men, we shall not ste to clinch the i 511.1.2 by voting for the man of our choice. All that the society has thne, or wishes to do, is to enable its members to take advantage of the coming election, by forcing to the front the most pressing needs of reform which are most essential to the general welfare of railway-workers. There is no party capital intended, unless it be to the (as vet unorganized) Labour Party. My parting word to Joseph Dakin, is this—if he cannot back out his in- ferences by more solid arguments,let him,as an outsider, both electorally and as a non-society man hold his peace. —Yours truly. 11. OGDEN. 5, Collin-street, Warrington, June Ist, 1892.

THE CHURCH AND TIIE FORTHCOMING ELECTION. Sir,—Now that a dissolutios is drawing near, with your permission I should like to call the attention of churchmen to a few facts concerning the Church and the two political parts ; their past treatment of her,their present attitude, and their future promises. Oae small class cries out Bring the Bishops out of the House of Lords." I venture to submit that the Bishops are the Radical element in that House : they are not present because they happen to be the sons of their fathers,they are not the "tenth transmitters of a foolish race," but are the only representatives of what we all long to see duly honoured, the aristoaracy of intellect. What we do want altering is their method of election, which is a pure farce. The Dean and Chapter meet to pray for the guidance of the Holy Spirit to enable them to make a choice. They receive a cove (retire from the Crown with one name (not much choice here) ; if they refuse to elect that person they are liable to the penalties of priemunire, which include con- fiscation of goods a9d banishment for life. Oh! that all Deans and Residehtiary Canons would incur these penalties ; they are a useless class, and cost about £3,000 a year to each diocese which is unfortunate enough to have them. We get on quite as well in the diocese of Liverpool without them, and Church work does not suffer by their absence. . . . .

I will point out briefly what in my opinion the church does need: (1) Brim'* the Bishops out of their palaces, which cause a great deal of useless expense. Let them live in houses with less stipends. Abolish Deans and Residentiary Canons, use these funds for Church work in large poor parishes, have a rearrangement of endow- ments, and remember that the Church is for the benefit of the people, and not of the parsons. Toe Churchmen of one shape of opinion who met in Sankey-st. a few days ago omitted to state whether the " interests of the Church " meant those of the people, or of the parsons. As the parsons who signed the postcard are those with the largest clerical incomes in the town, and the very insignificant laymen who profess to be the Churchmen of the town are all .Tories, we can only conclude that this is a Tory dodge to catch the Church vote, and those par- sons are clinging like grim death to their loaves and fishes. One reverend gentleman grew rather hysterical on the subject of religious education. The Church has borne the burden of education for a long time now ; she has taught the nation the duty of educat- ing her children. Let Churchmen rejoice that the nation acknowledges this duty and mot put themselves in op- position to the work. The parsons do not care a straw about religious education, for nine-tenths of them leave it to the teachers: what they do care for and fear is popular control of day schools and loss of personal influence. What has Mr. Gladstone done for the Curch ? His epis- copal appointments have been without exception men of exemplary piety, of profound learning, noble leaders of men. Lord Beaconsfield passed the Public Worship Regulation Act and appointed Bishop Ryle, the admitted failure. The Public Worship Regulation Act has done the Church very great harm, and even Lord Beaconsfield deeply regretted Bishop Ryle's appointment as a bait to catch the Orange vote (see "London Guardian" for May 25th, 1892). Lord Salisbury has flung the same kind of bait, by appointing the mediocrity Bardsley to follow the giant Harvey Goodwin : how do the good people of Carlisle diocese approve this appointment? Mr. Glad- stone purified the Irish Church by her disestablishment. She was so thoroughly out of touch with the people that ,a less drastic measure wouid hay e been useless ; now she has got rid of the drones, and has taken a fresh lease of spiritual life.

The Tory party invite the Church vote by professing to protect the interests of the Church (the old story of " Codlin's the friend, not short.") The Tory party do not care for the Church, but long for the Church vote ; the frequenters of the Tory club in Warrington are not Churchmen in reality, they are not communicants, they are bigoted and ignorant Orangemen intel!ectually the lowest class of politicians, for theirs is the ignorance which refuses to learn. The Newcastle progra=e, on

which this election is to be fought, contains no single thing which will harm the Church. Looking at the past, therefore, and considering the people's interests, not the parson's, the duty of Churchmen is clear ; Churchmen I mean men who are communicants and put their religion first, not their polities, men who think for themselves, and are not led by the nose, men who are not afraid to vote acording to their conscience, and are in no fear of the voice of blatant ignorance. One of these, I trust, is your humble servant, who is proud to call himself
A RADICAL CHURCHMAN.
THE "ALLIANCE NEWS" ON A LDERMAN HARRISON.
The following is the concluding portion of an article in the "Alliance News" on "A Warrington Alderman's definitions of drunkenness" :

It is not at all surprising, if after sitting, as it were, at the feet of this W arrington Gamaliel, the Chief Constable found his situation rather a jolly one. First, the baffled official excused his action with the plea that the summons had been ordered and issued, not by him, but by the magistrates. And then he went on to add that "he should be very careful in future how he took out summonses on his own responsibility." Behold how admirably Alderman Harrison provided for fair play to the publican! When we say he provided it, we are far from affirming that he was at all aware that he was doing so. After studying the report of his remarks, we hardly feel competent to fix any limit to the amount of that which he may not be aware of. But whether he meant it or not, truly this may be re- commended as a sure 'receipt. Bother the police sufficiently, and then the law-breakers are sure to get fair play. Discourage all endeavour on the part of the police force to bring law-breakers to account, and thus you secure fair play in future, without being biased one way or the other! In talking about law-breakers, we are not speak- ing quite without book. All this flimsy distinction between intoxication and drunkenness—between being nearly drunk, under the influence of liquor, and being quite drunk—between being able to know without caring what one is doing, and being neither able to know nor to care—would be swept away, like so much cobweb before Betty's broom, almost anywhere but in Warrington. According to the latest decision Of the judges, it is an offence against the law to have a drunken man on licensed premises, even if ha have got drunk wholly else- where. Of course, to fill a sober man till he is drunk is no less a case of law-breaking. And to pretend that a man so plied with liquor that he can commit almost any outrage without caring what he is doing, is not drunk, unless also he is so insensible as to be fit to do little but lie down and snore, is a pretence that no judicial tribunal in a state to know what it is doing (excepting, of course, that of which Alderman Harrison seems to be the prevalent luminary) would lend countenance to for a moment. To hold, as that luminary does, that a drinkseller may have no indisputable knowledge that a person served with drink is drunk, whilst yet that person is so "nearly drunk" that he does not care what crime he commits, may be con- sidered fair play, but only by inconsiderate persons. And to make it difficult for a police force to do its duty, by insising on all this prepos- terous length of tether, called fair play, being granted to the publican, may perhaps suit the latitude of Warrington, but we should scarcely think it could be done in a public court in any other locality. PROTEST BY THE TEMPERANCE

div.head: FEDERATION.
div.p: FEDERATION.

At a largely-attended meeting of the Warrington Temperance Federation, which was held in the Horsemarket-st. Cocoa Rooms,on Thursday evening, amongst othet matters considered was the subject of Alderman Harrison's remarks at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday week; and the following resolution was unanimously adopted :—"That this meeting of the committee of the Warrington Tem- perance Federation strongly protests against the language used by Alderman Harrison, a magistrate of the borough of Warrington,in the Borough Police Court, on the 23rd of May,regarding it as calculated to defeat the ends of justice by discouraging the Chief Constable and the members of the police force in the execution of their duty."

div.head: INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.
ARRIVAL oF THE CHARTER.

The long expected Charter of incorporation of Widnes was receined at Widnes Town Hall on Monday, having' been sent in the ordinary way by post. It was accompanied by the follow- ing letter addressed to •• H. S. Oppenheim, Esq., acting town clerk, Town Hall, Widnes : Whitehall, 28th May, '1892. Sir, I am directed by Mr. Secretary Matthews to transmit to you the enclosed letters patent under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom granting a Charter of Incorpora- tion to the Borough of Widnes, together with a financial statement of the expenses incurred in connection with the issue of the Charter, and an order upon her Majesty's Paymaster General for the balance (£1 65.) due to you ; and I am requested that you will be good enough to acknowledge the receipt of these documents. I am, sir, your.obe.dient servant, E. Leigh Pemberton," It appears that several days ago Mr. Oppenheim had fiarwarded a cheque for £llO to cover the customary fees, and the balance mentioned is returned out of that sum. The fees have thus amounted to £lOB 14s. In the charter are set out the 16 clauses contained in the amended scheme pub- ashed in this journal early in April ; and then there is provided that Mr. Frederick Herbert Gossage, who is at present chairman of the Local Board, shall be the , provisional Mayor for the purposes of the first election. In case Mr. Gossage should be unable to perform the duties,then Mr. H. Wade Deacen,C.C. is to act. Mr. Op- Penheitu is appointed acting Town Clerk. By the provi- sions of the charter Widnes is now converted into a borough, but the Local Board will continue to carry on the aot'airs of the town until the Ist of November when the first municipal election will take place. The Town Council will meet on November 9th,when the Mayor ard Aldermen will be elected. The Local Board consists of 15 members, the Council will be formed of 18 councillors and six aldermen. The councilors will be elected from six wards, viz, Farnworth, Halton, Simms Cross Victoria Waterloo, and West Bank, whose area and population have been previ- ously described. The Councillors receiving the smallest number of votes in each ward will be called upon to retire in 1893, those receiving the next smallest in 1894, and the remaining councillors in 1895. Tbe three aldermen receiving the smallest number of votes will retire in 1895. and the other three in 1898. The Local Board of Widnes was constituted in 1885, Mr. Wm. Gossage being the first chairman, and his son. Mr. Fred Gossage, will, without doubt, be the first Mayor of the town. In that year the rateable value of Widnes was £3),564 ; it is now £140,585. At the census pre- vious to 1855 the population was 6,893, and there are now 30,011 inhabitants in the district. The area of the borough is 3,039 acres.

The seven Protestant officials of the Corporatioq are entitled to know against whom this charge is made. I say that such a charge is a foul libel at once on the Roman Catholic and Nationalist members of the Corporation and on the Protestant offi- Mals of the Corporation,andl have no hesitation in char- acterizing it as such. Your correspondent also says that I am wrong in stating that the Corporations of Derry and Belfast do not employ Roman Catholics. If lam wrong I shall be the first to acknowledge my mistake. Let him tell me their names, what posts they hold, and what salaries they receive, and I shall at once inquire and report the result through your columns, if you will per- mit me to do so. • But even if it be true that Roman Catholics are employed by the Protestant Corporations of Derry and Belfast,. it would not weaken the force of the argument derived from the action of thc Roman Catholic Corporation of Dublin. It would only go to show them that there was less bigotry in Protestant Ulster than I supposed, a fact which I for one would rejoice to learn.—Yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON. 52 Fitzwilliam-square, Dublin, May 31,1392.

div.head: _ DR. HOUSTON AND HIS ASSAILANTS.
div.p: _ DR. HOUSTON AND HIS ASSAILANTS.
DR. P.*NTOUL WRONG AGAIN.

Dr. Houston' latest speeches in Warrington seem to have excited as much interest in Ireland as they did on this side of the Irish Sea. As usual, Dr. Rentoul has rushed in, and made himself ridiculous by the exercise of his extraordinary faculty for misrepresenting everybody whom he professes to quote; and as usual, as will be seen from the an- nexed correspondence, he has got his knuckles well rapped. DR. RENTOUL'S LETTER.

" Sir,—l see in the " Freeman's Journal "of yester- day a report of Dr. Houston's meeting at Warrington, in which he says---' They would no doubt have speakers like Dr. Rentoul paid for coining there telling them, &c.' Permit me to say that I never received directly or in- directly one farthing or one farthing's worth for politi- cal speaking or political work of any kind in my life. And just as little have I benefited indirectly by politics, as my sole source of income is my practice at the English Bar, and the bulk of my clients are Radicals. I am very sorry on Dr. Houston's own account that he is obliged to descend to a statement of the kind. On my way from my holiday in Ireland I addressed a meeting in Warrington for my friend and fellow-barrister Mr. Pierpoint, and I believe I addressed it without one un- kind allusion either to Dr. or Mrs. Houston.—Yours truly.'? .
DR. HOUSTON'S REPLY.
TO EDITOR OF FREEMAN NATIONAL PRESS.

52, Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin, May 31. Dear Sir,—A letter appears in your issue of yesterday, dated May 27, from Dr. Rentoul, in which, with an inaccuracy fast becoming proverbial, he writes :—" I see in the ' Freeman's Journal' of yesterday a report of Dr. Houston's meeting at Warrington, in which he says, • They, would, no doubt, have speakers like Dr. Rentoul paid for coming there telling them, &c.,' " and he con- descendingly and compassionately adds, " I am very sorry on Dr. Houston's own account that he is obliged to descend to a statement of the kind." I have your excellent report of my speech before me, and there is nothing in it from beginning to end to warrant Dr. Rentoul in making such a statement, nor did I, upon that or any other occasion, ever refer to his being paid for political work. His pity for my supposed fallen condition is therefore quite misplaced. An allu- sion was indeed made to the subject of payment by another speaker at the meeting which might bear the interpretation that Dr. Rentoul had been paid. But I am sure that he will accept fully and frankly, as I do, Dr. Rentoul's assertion that he has never received any remuneration for political work.—l remain, yours faith- fully, ARtaftlll HOINTON. As the "Dublin Mail" had copied Dr. Rentoul's letter, and commented upon it, Dr. Houston sent the following letter, which appeared in the " " of Wednesday last :

div.head: TO THE EDITOR OF THE MORNING AND EVENING MAIL.
div.p: TO THE EDITOR OF THE MORNING AND EVENING MAIL.

Suffice it to say that before abus- ing and insulting a fellow-citizen as you have done, it would have been well if you had first ascertained whether the averments upon which your indictment was founded were true. Dr. Rentoul's colossal inaccu- racy is perfectly well known, and you had only to turn to the report of my speech referred to by him to see that there was not one fragment of foundation for the asser- tion that I used the words he puts into my mouth. I have the honour to be—Your obedient servant, ARTIE:TR HOUSTON.

52, Fitzwilliam square, Dublin, May 31st, 1892. [We are glad to see Dr. Houston is in full lighting trim for the general election, and his Dublin friends will watch his candidature in England with great interest. That he should win, however, is another natter.—ED. MORNING AND EVENING MAIL.] PROTESTANT OFFICIALS AND THE DUBLIN CORPORATION.

A more important issue has been raised by the argument in favour of Home Rule which Dr. Hous- ton founded on the appointment of several Protest- ant officials by the Corporation of Dublin. "The Daily Express" of Dublin, a Unionist organ, com- menting on a letter on the subject sent by a corres- pondent signing himself Truth" says Dr. Houston, Q.C., is naturally ambitious to get a seat in ?ornament. It is a very legitimate object, but wholly unattainable in Ireland. His ability is acknow, ledg,ed, and is turned to account when the help of a sound lawyer is required, but he does not possess the qualities which would commend him to a constituency whose ideas of fitness accord with those of the National Federation. Although he has posed as a Protestant Home Ruler, and may be supposed to have special claims on that account, he has not the stamp of Mr. Healy's approval, and, perhaps, does not desire to have it. There is no place reserved for him in the ranks of the Irish Parliamentary Party, and it is probably thought that the accession of a member, who is not up to the matk in vituperative power, and may be suspected of having some independent spirit, would add no strength to I it; although it would eive it more respectability. ' lie has been honoured, however, with an invitation to contest the borough of Warrington, as "an independent Gladstor,ian Liberal," like that flexible politician, Mr. Dickson. In a speech delivered on Monday last, which has been ignored by his friends in Ireland, he enlightened the electors by the remarkable statement that "the best positions under the Dublin Corporation are held by Tories and Protestants." He wished, of course, to dispel the idea that there is anY reason to apprehend sectarian or political intolerance in the event of Home Rule being granted, and to cast discredit upon the evidence which has been given to the contrary. Our correspondent, however, exposes the fallacious character of this state- ment."
Dr. Houston's reply is n most effective one, and appears in the Thursday's Dublin "Express" as follows :
; "HOME RULE FICTIONS." TO TIIE EDITOR OF THE DAILY EXPRESS.

Sir,—On my return from Warrington this morning I was somewhat surprised, perhaps flattered, to find that my name had been figuring rather prominently in the Dublin Press. From your paper, at all events, I do not anticipate any intentional unfair play. I was sorry, therefore, to see in the " Express " of last Saturday a leading article, founded upon a letter headed "Home Rule Fictions," referring to a statement said to have been made by me in a speech delivered at W'arringtcn on the 23rd inst., that "the best positions under the Dublin Corporation are held by Tories and Protestants." I think your correspondent must have taken this passage from the excellent, but necessarily condensed, report of my speech given in the "Freeman's Journal and Nitional Press" of the 26th inst. That report does not give the details into which I went on the occasion. Before I go into those details, let me observe that what I was urging on my audience was this, that they should judge of the con- duct likely to be exhibited by the Roman Catholics of Ireland towards their Protestant fellow-countrymen after Home Rule was granted, not by vain fears and unworthy suspicions, but by observing what was their conduct where they were posseSsed" of power already. " By their fruits shall ye know them." I.therefore turned to the Corporation of Dublin, an admittedly Roman Catholic and Nationalist body, so far as the overwhelm- ing majority of its members aro concerned, and I pointed out that. instead of shutting the 'doors of pro- motion and emolument in the face of Protestanrs and Tories, it elected the best men, irrespective Of sect and party. In proof of this, I think I took as eXamples Sir Charles Cameron (the medical officer of health, executive sanitary officer and city analyst), whose salary is £l,OOO a year ; Thomas Fri-, Esq., J.P. (the city treasurer, whose salary is £5OO a year) ; :spencer Harty, Esq , C.E. (the city engineer and borough surveyor), whose salary is £BOO a year ; J. Andrews, C.E. (one of the assistant engineers); Mervyn P. Crofton, Esq.. (super- visor .of waterworks). I only mentioned these five. They were enough for my purpose ; and on reference to the report of my speech in the local papers I find that I stated that they were Protestants, and some Tories, by which statement I abide. It appears that there are, in fact, seven Protestants officials, however, according to your correspondent, and of these gentlemen he speaks in the following terms Of the seven, two are Protest- ant Home Rulers, and one resigned Freemasonry before his appointment, and the remaining four would, I have little doubt, vote to a man for a Nationalist—they dare not do otherwise." I call upon your correspondent, who signs himself " Truth," to name the gentleman whom he thus classifies. If it be true that two of them are Pro- testant Home Rulers, I sincerely rejoice at it, for it proves one of two things—either that a man's religion is no drawback to his advancement under a Roman Catholic body, or that under such a body greater importance is attached to the question of politics than that of religion, which is quite enough for the purpose of my argument, namely, that under a Home Rule Government in Ireland, as all the world over, people would not be divided according to their religious convictions, but according to th irpolitical convictions. Who the gentleman is that is said to have resigned Freemasonry before his appointment—observe he is not said to have been required to do so—l do not pretend to know, but I do know that it is not the most highly paid of the officials I have mentioned, for Sir Charles Cameron is a very prominent member of that

div.head: DR. AND MRS. HOUSTON.
div.p: DR. AND MRS. HOUSTON.

The Dublin " Figaro " comments this week in the following lively style upon the Liberal can- didate for Warrington :—But the supreme con- test will be in Warrington, where Greek meets Greek in deadly vengeance .when :that villainous Tory, yclept Pierpoint, tries conclusions with Gladstone's confidant and champion crusher, Arthur Houston, Q.C., Irish Solicitor-General in prospectu. Now, • Warrington is a typical labour constituency, and, consequently, when the election comes off (Quad .Di avertanfl for a time at least), the eyes of that hackneyed article,known as the civilised globe, are bound to be rivetted in grim earnest on Warrington and Houston. Arthur is, himself, brimful of enthusiasm on the subject, and his heart it is to be hoped will not much longer be weary, weary waiting for the day. Houston, QC., is a tidy, smug-faced little man,reminding you instinctively of a sedate parson in a wig and gown. He is a good speaker,and enjoys a considerable prac- tice at the Bar. He is, in the best sense,a man of the world, who can take genuine enjoyment out of life; and at the Gaiety theatre there is no more familiar figure than the genial doctor, with his quiet, unobtrusive manner, and his smoothly- chiselled face. But Arthur Houston is, par excellence, a politician, in a limited way. Ile was one of the Pillars of the Protestant Home Rule Association in its halcyon days, and at the periodical gatherings of this highly influential body, he was able to find a congenial nome and resting-place to ventilate his views on all the ..ning questions of an hour. Trained in such wise in this pakestrum of oratory and thorough-going Liberalism rolled into one, Houston appears on the ramparts of Warrington with the time-honoured mantle of Grattan over his shoulders, and the banner of the Grand Old Parliamentary Spider float- ing in the air. And against such a combination let the Tories be abashed, and Pierpoint hide his diminished head, his ignominy and shame. " The Lighthouse." a London shipping journal, has the following reference to Dr. and Mrs. Houston: —An Irish correspondent informs me that, if War- rington does not return Mr. Houston at the General Election, we shall have discarded the best man , Ireland has ever sent over to contest a seat in this country. My correspondent adds, "Houston is quite good enough to win a "Grand National." This in itself is a big recommendation. The Mr. Houston, I may remark, who is contesting Warrington, is not the Liverpool shipowner of that name, but a very able Irish Q.C., whose name and fame in Dublin are as well-known as the strawberry gardens. Further, my correspondent adds, "and Mrs. Houston with her graceful and charming presence and lovely voice would charm a bird off a tree." As far as my recollection goes, I do not think there is auch a thing as a tree in Warrington, but I hope this will not discourage Mrs. Houston, as, so long as she can charm the election birds out of their nests and make them fly to the polling booth, her duty as a dutiful and charming wife will be performed. "The Dublin Evening Telegraph "of Wednesday last says :—" The number of Protestant Home Rulers who are contesting seats in England at the General Election is a gratifying evidence of the nature of the tie which this great question is likely to create between the two peoples. It is not long since it would have been considered farcical to sug- gest that the day would come when Irish Home Rulers would be welcomed as candidates in English constituencies. The day has come, how- ever. Dr. Houston and others are already in the field. The latest accession is Mr. W. M. Cook. an Ulster Protestant, who is to contest Wandsworth as a Home Ruler. If one of the boroughs of London returns a Protestant Homo Ruler from Ulster it will be. a remarkable object lesson from the English pepple who are now appealed to on the Ulster ques- tion."

PROPOSED CRICRET Cuurs.—A meeting was held on Monday evening, in order to form a cricket club for Lymm. The Rev. J. T. Collins occupied the chair. The Rev. G. W. Guest was elected president, Mr. Roddy, secretary, and Mr. T. Ardin, treasurer. It was decided to look out for a fieid and to arrange a few matches for the season. DEATH OF Mn. THOMASON.—The death of Mr. Thoma- a well-known tradesman of Lymm, took place on Satur- day morning, at two o'clock. 'The deceased gentleman had been suffering for some time from cancer. He was taken ill some five weeks ago, but a few days since seemed to be very much better. On Friday he caught cold, and died on Saturday morning. Mr. Thomason (who was for many years a mem- ber of the Local Board) was respected by all, and a large circle of friends feel his loss very deeply. He was attended duling the illness by Dr. B-rabazon. His fune .1 took place on Tuesday, in the Parish churchyard. There was a large attendance, which included Mr. Saville, Mr. Brown, Mr. Rowson, Mr. P. Warburton,Mr. J. Thomason (son of the deceased) and also his wife, Mr. Bruce, Mr. Peason, Mr. nekton. Mr. L. Jackson, Mr. Forest, Mr. H. Harrison, Mr. Wol- ford, Mr. Henshall, Mr. Whitelegge, and about 16 cholars of the Sunday school at which deceased was Superintendent. The service at the graveside was con- ducted by the Rev. Mr. Southwall. The deceased gentleman was 63 years of age, and was a Primitive Methodist.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

-- THE HORSE Swig INN BOWLING CUM.—The members of this club, to the number of 54, had a picnic to the Stocks Inn, Padgate, on Saturday afternoon, to play a main of bowls for money and other prizes. The game was 11 up, the final round resulting-as follows :—First prize, copper kettle, Mr. P. Collier ; second prize, 55., Mr. H. Shaw : third prize, 2s. 6d., Mr. T. Unsworth. CRICKET Ccun.—A. meeting was held at the Board School, on Monday evening, to form a cricket club in ' connection with the school. There was a good atten- dance, and Mr. 'Cawthorne, the headmaster of the school, and promoter of the club, presided. About 16 members joined. Mr. Cawthorne was elected captain and treasurer, and Mr. William Sanderson secretary. TER BOARD Scnoot..—The report of the above school has been received from the Education Department. Con- sidering the various changes which have taken place with respect to the appointment of a new schoolmaster, new infant mistress, kc., it is a most gratifying one, the total amount of grant being for the scholars £B6 145., (or only about £1 less than the previous year). The total amount of grant received; including that for the pupil teacher, was over £9O.
g?.IDEMIC OF SCARLET FEVER.

Scarlet fever is rapidly spreading in Warrington and may now be said to have reached the character of an epidemic. There are over sixty cases at present in the fever hospital two-thirds of which have been received during the past week. A ver large number of the cases are from the streets off Bewsey-road, and in the part recently added to the borough in Orford Ward, beyond the Jockey Inn.

div.head: SETTLEMENT OF THE DURHAM STRIKE.
div.p: SETTLEMENT OF THE DURHAM STRIKE.

The Durham coalowners and the federated workmen having accepted the offer of the Bishop of Durham to , mediate in the present dispute, a representative of each , side met his lordship on Wednesday at Aukland Castle with a view of arranging a settlement. After a long interval, the owners agreed Co accept 10 per cent. re- duction, thus ending the strike. The result was hailed with delight by all parties. Reports from various parts of the country show that the result of Wednesday's conference has been ieceived with great satisfaction. Arrangements have been made for a meeting in Newcastle between the coalowners' committee and the federation board, to discuss arrange- ments to be made for restarting the pits. div.head: TRAGIC OCCURRENCE. DEATH OF A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER.
div.p: TRAGIC OCCURRENCE. DEATH OF A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER.

In unusual and melancholy domestic tragedy has occurred in Warrington this week. The daughter of Mr. Fletcher, of 6 George-street, Bawsey-road, was ill of consumption, and the medical man pro- nounced her to be dying. When the girl's mother discovered that this melancholy event must happen she was so overcome with grief that she bursted a blood vessel and expired before the death of her daughter took place, this occurring soon after. The widower as may be imagined, is bowed down in the deepest sorrow under his crushing double affliction, and is the subject of the greatest sympathy amongst his neighbours and friends.

div.head: NEW LOCAL RAILWAY.
div.p: THE NEW LOCAL RAILWAY.

On Thursday the Examiner on Standing Orders of the House of Commons certified that the Stand- ing Orders had been complied with in respect to the bill of the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and,East Coast Railway Company, which contemplates the con- struction of several branch railways and the acquisi- tion of the North Sea Fisheries harbour and dock on the Lincolnshire coast. The bill has already passed through the House of Lords, and is an ex- tension of the line authorised last year for the con- struction of a trunk line from the east to the west coast, the first sod of which is to be cut on Tuesday next at Chesterfield Mrs. Arkwright will perform the ceremony and will be supported by the Duke of Newcastle and the county gentry. Invitations to the ceremony have been sent out to those hold- ing leading public offices and to the representatives of the press along the proposed route of the rail- way.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
The monthly meeting of this council will be held at the Town Ball, on Tuesday evening next, and the following matters amongst others will be dealt with. •
TAN DISCAARCIE OF A SCAVENGER.
Councillor Dixon has again given notice that he will ask the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee for the particulars why a man named Sutton, who was a scavenger, was discharged.
LONGFORD "GASES."

The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contain a report by Mr. A. Norman Tate, F.1.C., F.C.S., &c., analytical and consulting chemist and consulting chemical engineer,in which he states that,in accordance witn instructions received from Mr. Long,din, he pro- ceeded to Longford on the 17th, and there inspected the " destructor " plant. He speaks of the general arrange- ment of the plant as being in every way convenient. The character of the furnaces he found to be admirably adapted for perfect combustion of the refuse, and, in short, the whole of his inspection of the works and examination of the gases, &c. evolved from the " Destructor "convinced him that the refuse was very .completely burnt without in any way eliminating any- thing that cold be considered noxious or offensive, and he considered all the arrangements of the plant very satisfactory. THH HOSPITAL.

The Sanitary Committee report that inasmuch as the period for the compulsory purchase of the plot of land adjoining the hospital will shortly expire, the Commit- tee are of opinion that it is desirable that steps should be taken for the purpose of acquiring the land, and Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the owner of the land having agreed to refer the question of the price to the single arbitration of Mr. W.Owen, the Committee have also agreed to this course.

THE NAVIGATION OF THE RIVER. The Rivers Committee have passed the following resolutions :—" That the Borough Surveyor be instructed to call the attention of the Liverpool Corporation to the necessity of removing the temporary line of pipes across the river as soon as possible after the supply from Vyrnvvy is carried through the permanent aqueduct at Fiddler's Ferry ;" and "that the Upper Mersey Navi- gation Commissioners be requested to substitute hooped painted casks for the wood buoys in the River between Bank Quay and Runcorn." ANOTHER USE FOR THE BATHS. Councillor R. T. Fairclough has given notice of the following motion :—" To consider the advisability of arranging the heating of the new bath so that it may be utilised for growing plants."
MARRIAGE OF MISS NELLIE BIRTLES
AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday morning there was a large and interested gathering at Wycliffe Church to witness the wedding which there took place of Mr. James Carter Bate, solicitor, of -Tarporley, and son of Mr. Roger Bate, C.C., to Miss Nellie Birtles, daughter of Mr. Thomas Birtles, photographer, Sankey-st., Warrington. The principal parties in the ceremony were driven from Legh House, the residence of Mr. Stales, and their departure was witnessed by a considerable gathering of spectators. The bride was accompanied by her father, and, on alighting at the church entrance, flowers were strewn in her pith by the Misses Carter, of Prodsham, daughters of Mr. Thomas Carter, and as she entered the church music suitable to the occasion' was rendered on the organ by Mr. W. 11. Payton. The bride's dress was of grey silk, trimmed with white passemeterrie and she carried a beauti- ful bouquet of stephanotis and myrtle, maidenhair and orange blossom. The bridesmaids were Miss Ada Birtles and Miss Bate and the Misses Lilie and Kittie Birtles, and Miss Dorothy Browne, a daughter of Councillor A. Browne. Miss Ada Birtles and Miss Bate were attired in cream 'muslin delaine, trimmed with green silk and wore white Tuscan hats trimmed with pink honeysuckle. They also carried bouquets composed of lilies and pink roses. Miss Lily and Miss Kitty Birtles were dressed in cream and yellow dresses with hats to match, and they carried pretty bouquets. The best man was Mr. John Birtles, brother of the bride. The Rev. J. Yonge was the offieiat- ng minister. - On leaving the church the " Wedding March " was played on the organ, and outside, the newly wedded pair were treated to the customary showeis of rice. There was afterwards a large company of invh,ed guests present at the wedding breakfast at Legh House, amongst them being Mr. Bate, C.C., Mrs. Bate and family, Mr. and Mrs. Birtles, Council- lor and Mrs. Browne, Mrs. and the Misses Carter, Mr. and Mrs. T. Bate, &c. It should be mentioned that the flowers, of which there was a fine display, had been forwarded by Mr. Tomkinson, of Willington Hall, the Liberal candidate fer the Eddisbury divi- sion. The bride's presents were very numerous and handsome and included a cheque, a piano, an oak dining table, a sideboard, &c. The bride and bride- groom left in the afternoon for London cc route for Hastings. WARRINGTON TRADES AND LADOUR COUNCIL. The annual demonstration promoted by this Council will be held next Saturday. There will be processien through the principal streets, starting from the vacant ground near Holy Trinity Schools. QUOITING MATCH.—WARRINGTON L. AND N.-W. v. BIRKENHEAD STANDARD. _ _

The above match was played on the ground of tbe former, on May 280, and resulted as follows : Warrington L. and N.-W., 294; Birkenhead Stan- dard, 278; majority for Warrington, 16. WHITSUNTIDE ARRA.NGEItIENTS. It will be seen from our advertising columns that special arrangements have been made with reference to the Whitsuntide Holidays by the L. and N.-W. Railway Campany, The Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company, The Isle of Man Steam Packet Company. The Belle Monte Pleasure Grounds will , be open as usual. I WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided. The valuer reported that he had been desired to make a re-valuation of the Friends School, renketh. In 1888 he reported that in his opinion the school premises would probably let as a private venture school at £l2O per annum, and that, legally, the assessment should follow the letting value. The Committee then con- sidered the matter and concluded to fix the assess- ment at £5O grvss, looking upon the school as a benevolent institution. Some discussion took place on this matter, and ultimately the Committee decided to fix the assessment of the schools at £lOO gross. •
LATEST NE WS.
TERRIBLE FIRE IN A MINE.

div.head: 500 MEN ENTOMBED.-361 LIVES LOST.
div.p: 500 MEN ENTOMBED.-361 LIVES LOST.

PRAGUE, WEDNESDAY. —Fire broke out yesterday in the Maria shaft of the famous Birkenberg Silver Mine, near Przibram. Some 400 men were at work at the time if the outbreak, the majority of whom were safely brought to bank. About 40, however, were cut off by flames. Rescue parties were organised as soon as pos- sible, and up to the present 14 dead bodies and a num- ber of men seriously injured have been brought out of the mine. The work of rescue still continues, and the fire has been subdued.

PRAGUE, WEDNESDAY, SEVEN P.m.—Later reports re- ceived here of the fire in the Birkenberg Silver Mine show that the disaster was even more serims than at first supposed. Of the 500 men who were at work in the mine, it is now known that 200 are still missing. So far the rescue parties have re- covered 25 dead bodies, and the same number of miners has been extricated alive, but their condition was so serious that they had all to be conveyed to the hospital. All those brought up dead had evidently been suffocr ted and three volunteers who were engaged in the work of rescue met their death in a similar manner. As far as can be ascertained at present the disaster was probably due to the reckless use by one of the miners of a naked light. On the other hand, a wild rumour has got abroad that the mine was wilfully set on fire. Little hope is entertained that the men who are still itnpri- soned in the workings will escape With their lives. Crowds of women and children are gathered round the pit's mouth, anxiously awaiting tidings of their hus- band's and father's ; and many heartrending scenes took place as the dead were brought to the surface.
HEARTRENDING SCENES.-ALL HOPE ABANDONED. _

PRAGUE, THURSDAY.—The work of rocovering: the bodies from the Berkeberg Silver Mine, near Przibram, continued uninterruptedly throughout the night. The scenes witnessed as the bodies were brought up and re- cognised were most heartrending. Many of those wait- ing in suspense at the pit's mouth had scarcely left the spot since Tuesday night, when the fire first broke out. Up to the present sixty-seven bodies have been recovered, and all hope for the missing, numbering about 150, has now been abandoned. No one could have lived in the suffocating atmosphere of the mine. Count Falkenhayn, Minister of Agriculture, arrived to-day from Vienna by special train and visited the scene of the disaster. VIENNA, THURSDAY.—The Lower House of the Reichs- rath to-day passed unanimously an urgency motion brought forward by Dr. Edward Suess calling upon the ' Government to make adequate provision for the sur- vivors of the miners who have perished in the terrible catastrophe at Przibram, and to cause to be erected a marble tablet perpetuating the names of the men who ' have so gallantly laboured at the risk of they lives at the work of rescue.

VIENNA, THURSDAY NlGHT.—According to the latest news from Przibram 361 miners are now missing, and are no doubt dead. Among them are five pupils of the Mining School at Przibram. This evening 112 bodies had been recovered.

LATEST. PRAGUE, FRIDAY.—The latest accounts now published here state that the number of lives lost through the fire in the Przilram Silver Mine will probably be found to reach 400. Large trenches have been dug in the church- yards at Przibram and Birkenberg„ capable of receiving 350 bodies, it being impossible to provide separate graves.
IIEETING OF WARRINGTON BINDSAIEN.

div.head: MUSIC IN TILE PARK.
div.p: MUSIC IN TILE PARK.

On Monday evening a meeting of the Committee of the newly-formed Warrington Association of Amateur Bands was held in the Committee room at the Town Hall. Councillor F. W. Monks presided,l in the absence of Mr. T. J. Downs, president of the Association. The Chairman mentioned that the Committee that was met there consisted of the bandmasters and one representative from each of the bands of Warrington, and it was thought that such a Committee would be able to manage the business of providing music in the Park, than the former Committee. The Corpo ration, he added, voted .V. 25 a year towards paying the bands which played in the Park, and a question they had to consider was as to the way in which they would raise any additional money that might be required. Collections had been made in the Park when the bands were playing, but this was found to be a rather disagree- able business,and the sums raised by it were very small, sometimes so low as 10d. or even 6d. in an evening. Some years ago subscriptions were raised by calling at various houses in the town, in which way .£l2 or £l3 were obtained. At that time, however, the Corporation only voted .£l2 10s.—Mr. J. Taylor (hon. secretary) said it was estimated that the number of peeple who were in the Park on Sunday when the Volunteer band was playing was about 2,000, yet only 2s. 103., and a piece of toffee (laughtor)—were placed in the collecting boxes. He thought the best way of raising extra money would be to get townspeople to promise subscriptions. Some further conversation took place on the subject, but ultimately it was left over till the committee could ascertain more clearly what sum of money would really be required.—The following programme for June of music to be played in the Park was then arranged June sth: Warrington United Band; 6th: Lehgue of the Cross, dancing; Bth: Warrington United; 12th : League of the Cross ; 13th : St. Paul's, dancing; 16th ; Cockhedge Mission; 19th; Messrs. Fletcher's and Coy a, Band; 20th : St. Paul's, dancing ; 23rd: League of t Cross;ie 26th: Volunteer; 27th : St. Paul's, dancing ; 30th: Brick-st. School.

ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT STOCKPORT. At Stockport, on Thursday, a married woman named Swann was proceeding to a factory, when she was shot in the head by Joseph Blood, who is supposed to have had some former acquaintance with her. Blood after- wards attempted suicide, but only succeded in wounding his temple. He said he would have finished it on Thurs- day but it was Derby Day, and he wanted to ace which horse won. Both the man and thc woman are expected to recover. • • •.•

Mary Fyldes, of Little John-st., was bound over to keep the peace.--John 94., Dock-st., failed to appear to a summons charging him with assaulting Mrs. Phillips, of Pear-St. He was fined 103. and oots.— Catherine Holland, aged .twelve, was convicted of steal- ing a pair of boots worth 2. 11d., the property of the Great Northern Boot Co., Albert-road. She was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. RUNCORN PEF TY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—BefOre Major Ilazlehurst and Mr. James Handley. . A BICYCLIST.—ThomaR Heath Barton was ordered to pay costs 4s. 6,1., for riding a bicycle without a lighted lamp on the 18th ult.. TRESPASSING.—WiIIiaM Hayes, of Frodshana, was CDR- victed of having on the 23th May trespassed in pursuit of game on land at Aston, in the joint occupation of John Rivies and others.—The defendant said his dog got beyond his control and he went into the covers after turn. A fine of ss. and costs 103. 6.1. was imposed. DRUNlC.—Michael McEver and Patrick Briscoe, Irish farm labourers, were each fined 5.3., including costs, for being drunk and disorderly. CERTIFICATE OF OCCUPATION.—David Watkins was summoned at the instance of James Farrington,inspector to Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, for causing or permitting a house at Weston Point to be occupied with- out having obtained a certificate of occupation.—Mr. Farrington said he believed the defendant had acted in ignorance, and a nominal penalty would' meet the case. Ordered to pay costs. COAL DEALERS AND THEIR SCALES.—FIenry Lacy and Edward Prince,coal dealers, were charged with hawking coal without having a scale and weights in their respec- tive carts. Inspector Hallard proved the case, and each defendant was fined 93. including costs. The Bench ; , considered there was no wilful attempt to evade the law.

CRICKET. Marylebone all out for 240 ; Oxford second innings all out for eight ; Middlesex, 229- for six wickets ; Surrey beat Somerset by 11 runs. THE CHOLERA. A ".Times "second edition, published on Friday, says that over 3,000 deaths from cholera have occurred at Srinagar. THE LATE ADMIRAL MAYNE. The funeral of the late Admiral Richard Mayne, M.P.. took place at Kensal Green Cemetery, yesterday, the burial service having been previously held at St. Peter's Kensington. FATAL RESULT OF A "LARK." A shocking affair occurred yesterday morning near Chorley, Lencashire. Two gamekeepers named Aspy, and Naylor, were watching for poachers, and a travell- ing watchmaker, named Henry Thompson joined them, and commenced larking with Nallor. Naylor's gun went off, and fatally shot Thomptmn through the head. Naylor is in custody. CHILD ROASTED IN ITS CRADLE. A shocking burning accident to a child named Wilkin- son, terminated fatally at Bolton yesterday morning. The little one was lying in its cradle suffering from a broken leg, and during the brief absence of its mDther, another child set fire to the cradle, and deceased was nearly roasted, its back and legs being dreadfully barned, and presented a shocking sight. YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past two o'clock. RIVER POLLUTION IN LANCASHIRE.—On the motion that the Standings Orders be suspended and the Mersey and Irwell Prevention of Pollution Bill be read a third time,—Sir H. JAMES opposed the suspension of the Standing Orders on the ground that without making an attempt to put in force the provisions of the Rivers Pot- lotion Act, 1876, the County Council of Lancashire had taken the extraordinary course of introducing this Bill. After some discussion, the House divided, and the motion for the suspension of the standing orders was carried by 71 to 6, amidst laughter. The Bill was then read a third time. THE JACKSON SLAVIN CASE.—The HOME SECRETARY, answering Mr. Cobb, said as to the prize fight which took place at the National Sporting Club, on May 31st, he had nothing to add to his answer ot yesterday, save that he was informed by the Commissioner that the police were not present on the occasion. After some formal business had been transacted the House adjourned till June 9th.

SUICIDE OF MR. J. CAVE WHITTLE. Early on Wednesday morning a lamplighter go- ing his rounds found at the corner of the Waterloo Dock, Liverpool, a man's coat, hat, and a pair of boots. He also discovered a piece of paper on which was written "Starving. God bless my child and mother. None better ever lived.--C." At two o'clock in the morning a police officer was in- formed of the matter, but after carefully searching the dock could find no further trace of anybody. There was a strong tide running at the time, and it is supposed that the owner of the clothes had jumped into the river off the pierhead. Subse- quently the clothes were identified by Mrs. Cave as those of her husband; William Cave. He was a mining engineer, lodging for the past five weeks at 69, Elizabeth-st. For some time he had been out of work, and had also been suffering from brain fever. The deceased, who went under the name of Mr.. "William Cave," was Mr. James Cave Whittle, r formerly a member of the Warrington Town Coun- cil. He was a son of the late Mr. Josiah Whittle, a prominent tradesman of Warrington, and also member of the Town Council for same years. Paris dogs are henceforth to be muzzled, as ManY 'fresh cases of madness have been reported. , Despatches from Honolulu state that a plot has been discovered, in which the conspirators sought the de- thronement of the Queen of the Sandwich Islands. Enoch Jones, a labourer, was, at Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, sentenced to eighteen years' penal servitude for having assaulted his daughter, at Eccleston, in April last. Mr. J. W. Hill, veterinary surgeon, St. Leonard's, - was on Monday awarded £5OO compensation for injuries received last October while travelling on the Great Western Railway. The new Olympia Circus in Liverpool was destroyed by fire at about midnight on Saturday, shortly after an audience who had listened to a lecture by Berry, the elc" hangman, had dispersed. The hearing of the claim to the Barnard peerage was concluded on Monday, when the Committee of Privileges of the House of Lords resolved to report that Mr. Henry de Vere Vane had made good his claim to the barony. Turkey having positively declined to allow Russia to erect in a commanding position a monument to the Russian soldiers killed in the war of 1878, a remote site has been selected in a valley six miles from San Stefano. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has UP- held the refusal by the Bishop of Norwich to institute the Rev. C. E. P. Boyer to the living of Branthanii,lll Suffolk, on the ground that Mr. Boyer had been nonna- ated to the benefice by Sir A. Dixie, a ROMall Catholic. Under a statute of Queen Anne a Roman Catholic is de- barred from exercising this patronage.
